Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Acting Minister of the Interior), moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 209, to amend the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act.
Explain.

When the former Act was passed, setting apart certain areas as forest reserves, the examination was not very full, close or accurate. It has been discovered since that there are in some cases, adjoining areas that should be added to these forest reserves and that in some cases, the present forest reserves included some agricultural land which should be taken from them. This Act is simply to amend the existing Act, enlarging the areas in some cases and in some cases taking some parts out of the reserves.

That is a
very important distinction. I have no objection to the proposal that the forest reserves should, be increased, but to introduce farm lands into the forest reserves is to propose something that will very much interfere with the object of the Act.
I think there is a very small portion to be so treated-only in one or two cases.
Even so.
What reserves are affected by the provision withdrawing from the reserves?

There are only one
or two cases, I think. I will tell my hon. friend a little later on. I have the details of each case and the number o.f square miles that it is proposed to add. It is only in one or two cases that anything is proposed to be taken from a reserve.

NAVAL FORCES OF THE EMPIRE-IMPERIAL SQUADRON AT GIBRALTAR.
speechtext:
I would call the attention of my right hon. friend who leads the House to a matter in regard to which I would like to get some information from him. In order to make my question intelligible I shall have to read a paragraph which I find in the United Empire for May, which just came to hand yesterday. Speaking of the recent speech of Mr. Churchill in regard to the organizing of a station at Gibraltar, the editor of the magazine says:
From that standpoint the most important part of the First Lord's statement was his declaration of the Admiralty's latest plan of Imperial co-operation. Its two parts are mutually dependent. On the assumption that the dominions would be willing to' provide the capital 6hips of a general service squadron, to be based at Gibraltar, the Admiralty suggests that they should direct their policies of local development to the provision of the ' necessary naval bases, dock-yards, crusiers, local flotillas, or other ancillary craft which would enable the Imperial squadron to operate for a prolonged period in any particular threatened theatre to which it might be sent.' To this squadron would be assigned the three prospective Canadian ships, together with the Malaya and New Zealand.
Then, on the next page, the editor goes on to say:
The reception of the Admiralty's proposal in the dominions was mixed. As regards Canada, where one would suppose that the Government would support it and the Opposition deprecate it, the announcement was followed by a sudden silence of the cables, which hitherto had been busy with the progress of the naval controversy. Only from' New Zealand was there any abundance of! comment which was thought likely to interest the British public. The getneral tenor was favourable to the scheme, though the selection of Gibraltar was not universally approved.
The question which I want to put to my right hon. friend is whether or not any official communication has been received from the Admiralty in regard to this intended project.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NAVAL FORCES OF THE EMPIRE-IMPERIAL SQUADRON AT GIBRALTAR.
speechtext:
In regard to what my right hon. friend first observed, I have nothing to do with and do not know anything about any communication to the press with respect to the seconding of his amendment. I did observe that the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Guilbault) had taken the floor before six o'clock, and it was yielded to my right hon. friend as a matter of courtesy. As far as the noise or the silence of the cables is concerned, I know nothing about it; I have nothing to do with their noise and I have nothing to do with their silence. In respect to the matter on which the right

hon. gentleman has asked a question, there has been no official communication from the Admiralty except in so far as the matter has been brought to the attention of the dominions throughout the speech of the First Lord of the Admiralty, from which I made a quotation last evening.

Passing from the navy on the sea to the navy on land, may I be allowed to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) whether a special rate was granted on the Intercolonial railway from Levis to Mont-magny to those desirous of attending a meeting there the day after to-morrow, and whether after it was granted, if it was granted, it was countermanded?

I do not know anything about the question at all. The management of the road is altogether from Moncton. I had a telegram from a gentleman in Quebec yesterday asking if I had countermanded the order, and I said that I did not know anything about it, and referred him to Moncton.
May I ask whether the hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) knows anything about it, as, I understand, he has been invited to attend the meeting?

I have not been invited to the meeting,- and I know nothing about the matter to which my hon. friend refers as far as the Intercolonial railway is concerned. It must be those Nationalists who voted with my hon. friend last night.
You got fourteen of them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to bring to the attention of the House a despatch from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, transmitting a question and answer in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom with respect to a matter that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition mentioned some time ago. The question was as follows:
Mr Hewins: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign Affiairs, whether his attention has been called to the case of three naturalized Canadians, formerly Russians, who upon a visit to Russia have been sentenced to Siberia for life on a charge of evading military service; whether, as stated in the Canadian House of Commons by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, on the 16th April, the British authorities have declined to interfere, or whether, as the late Canadian Prime Minister asserted, it is the right and duty of the British Government to protect persons possessing Canadian nationalisation.
Secretary Sir Edward Grey: His Majesty's Government have no information on the sub-
Mr. BORDEN.
jeot. They could not, however, claim to protect Russian subjects, when within the limits of the Emperor's dominions, from any consequences attaching to them for breach of the daws of Russia, whether they had been naturalised in Canada or in this country. The law of Russia would, in such cases, be the governing law, and no question of difference between British or Canadian nationality would arise.

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I wish to ask the hon. Postmaster General whether he intends to establish a rural mail service in the county of Montcalm, as I know he is well disposed to do all that which is fair and reasonable in the interest of the electors, in all the counties indistinctly. I have received from my electors numerous requests to the effect of establishing this service, and especially from those who live , in the parish of Saint-Jacques, beginning at the brook. There is, along that road, a great number of electors who are all unanimous in asking for that service. They are ready to pay the charges and expenses necessary, and the service in question would be a great benefit to them.
Have they made that request long ago?

Pretty long ago, that is before the new Administration came to power, and since then the request was reiterated to the post office inspector at Montreal. That. part of the parish is the richest, and its inhabitants would 'be very glad to hear that the Government will do them justice.
If the hon. minister wants them to make the request over again, they are ready to do so.
I hope the minister will not consider the fact that this is being asked by a Liberal. The majority of that parish has even voted against your humble servant. There are more Conservatives than Liberals along that road. However, I >do not think that the Postmaster General will punish those electors because they are so unfortunate as to be represented by a Liberal, and I hope he will soon take 'this matter into serious consideration.

I must say that this
is the first time the matter is submitted to me. So far, the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) has sent me no correspondence about it nor did he call my attention to it in the House. I must say- and I hope both sides of the House will bear testimony in my behalf

that I have never stopped to consider what was the political party adhered to by those concerned, or the fact that they were represented by a Conservative or by a Liberal,

when I was called upon to take a decision on such a question. So true is this, that 1 was even congratulated for so doing.
That is your duty. You have done what it was your duty to do.
Then I have done my duty.
It is your duty.

We are dealing with
one question, and the hon. member should not try to raise another one at the same time. I wish especially to point out that, in the province of Quebec, this question of postal roads should be considered more closely than it is at present, and I would be glad if it were.
If, in the big and beautiful parish of Saint-Jacques-de-l'Achigan, the establishment of a postal road is desired, I shall be very glad to help them as much as I can towards realizing such improvement.

The public lose nothing by this amendment, as it provides

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 211, to amend the Criminal Code.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill, which contains thirty-three sections, proposes to amend different dispositions of the Criminal Code, one of the principal dispositions dealt with is that relating to the carrying of arms or weapons upon the person. In this regard it is proposed so to amend the provision with regard to obtaining what is called a certificate of exemption from the prohibition of carrying concealed weapons, that such certificate shall be procurable from certain police officers instead of from justices of the peace.
What is the present state of the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At present a person is prohibited from carrying weapons unless he has a certificate of exemption from the provisions of the Act, which may be obtained from any justice of the peace. The proposed amendment seeks to limit the power of granting these certificates of exemption, which under the amendment are called permits, to the police in the different cities or localities, and leaving the poweT to justices of the peace only in localities where there are no such police officers. It has been thought better that the power should be invested in some specific officer or officers who would be responsible for the carrying out of the law, and not left to the justices of the peace gen-

erally. Perhaps the most important modification in connection with these restrictions of the right to carry firearms consists in the introduction of a provision to prohibit the sale of weapons of this kind-that is to say, pistols, sheath knives, bowie knives, daggers, stilettos, metal knuckles, skull crackers, and other offensive weapons-except to persons who have a permit to carry them. I think it is evident that we are coming to have a very large increase in the number of crimes of violence, whidh I think may he directly attributed to the general carrying of arms of this kind. While our population is increasing, being fed by constant streams of immigration-in which, generally speaking, we rejoice-it is coming to contain, I think, and regrettably so, a larger proportion of persons with regard to whom it is unsafe and certainly undesirable that the procuring of weapons of this kind should be as easy as it is under present conditions.
Can any person possessing a permit carry an unlimited number of weapons ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No person is entitled to carry such firearms without a permit. The section has not gone into the question of what quantity a man would be entitled to buy. With regard te the prohibition of sale, I may say that there is an exception to its application in the case of a bona fide sale by manufacturers or wholesale people to persons keeping stores where these things are sold. Perhaps we might consider at a later stage whether it is desirable that ue should define what number of firearms any individual can carry. The requirement provides that each of these sales shall be registered by the vendor, and that he shall register upon the permit presented to him the fact of sale.
Is there any provision for the limitation of the age of the individual to whom these firearms may be sold ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is in this section no limitation as to age; but the person must have a permit.
Would the sale of a revolver to a child ten years of age, for instance, be permitted ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If he had a permit, it would under this section, but he cannot get a permit. The provision with regard to sale is that you shall not sell to any person who has not a permit. The provision with regard to the granting of the permit is as follows:
Upon sufficient cause being shown, any officer of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police or commissioner of Dominion police or superintendent of provincial police or stipendiary or district magistrate or chief constable of Mr. DOHERTY.
any pity, incorporated town or district municipality may grant any applicant therefor, as to whose discretion and good character he is satisfied, a permit in form 76, for such period not exceeding twelve months as he deems fit.
There is no provision as to age, but one may safely assume that such an officer would not issue a permit to a child. Moreover, there is a separate and distinct provision in the Code at present under which the sale of firearms to persons under 16 years of age is prohibited, without regard to whether or not a permit has been issued,
The next section deals with the selling of pistols, airguns or firearms of any kind to minors, so it is obvious that persons under 16 years of age are subject to prohibition without regard to permit.
The next provision increases the penalty for the violation of section 150 of the Code I do not think it calls for any special explanation at the present moment.
Section 7 deals with the offering for sale of instructions or medicines represented to be a means of preventing conception or of causing abortion or miscarriage, and the advertising of medicines for the restoring of sexual virility.
Under the next section, which amends section 213 of the Code, any person is guilty of an offence who seduces or has illicit connection with any woman or girl previously chaste and under the age of 21 years, who is in his employment. Under the law as it stands at present, the words ' in a factory, mill, workshop or store ' are included, and it is proposed to strike these words out, making the offence consist in seduction of or illicit connection with any girl under the age of 21 years, of previously chaste character, who is in the employment of the seducer.
Section 9 deals with what is generally spoken of as the white slave traffic. The purpose of it is to make, in some respects, more severe and generally more easily enforcible the provisions of the law imposing punishment upon people who traffic in vice. These provisions, I may say, are practically the provisions of the English Act of last year; to that subject are devoted sections 9, 10, 11 and 12. They prescribe penalties for the keeping of bawdy houses, for the procuring of women for prostitution, and upon persons who seek to derive profit from the propagation of vice, more particularly . by the prostitution of women. There is also a provision intended to make the criminal law reach persons who lease their properties for use as houses of prostitution.
The next section is one extending to persons who lease gambling devices the provisions which now apply to persons who import, make, buy and sell such devices.
The next amendment provides punishment for the offence of deserting wife and

children. It is not proposed to alter the law as it now stands which makes it an offence, and prescribes the punishment for that offence, to desert wife or children where the effect of such desertion is to endanger their lives or health. It is proposed to add a section making such desertion an offence, even though it does not seriously endanger life and health, where the party deserting leaves his wife and children in want, and where the abandonment is without lawful excuse. The punishment provided for this latter offence is not so great as the punishment provided under the section ol the law' as it now stands.
The next section also deals with that subject, making provision in regard to the evidence of marriage that shall be necessary in such cases, and providing that the fact of acknowledgement and public cohabitation between man and woman shall be sufficient proof of the marriage of the persons in question. This is deemed necessary because such cases arise very frequently. They occur often in regard to newly arrived immigrants, where legal evidence of the marriage is difficult to obtain.
The next section makes it an offence for the husband or the wife who deserts his or her consort, at the time of the desertion, or subsequently, to steal anything belonging to his or her consort. As the law stands at present, the stealing by a husband or a wife, during cohabitation is not actually a crime. The case that is sought to be reached by this amendment is the case where either party is just about to abandon the other with the intent of deserting, and stealing takes place, that is, strictly speaking, during cohabitation.

How many
clauses are there in this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Thirty-three. The next section, 16, has for its purpose to make applicable the provisions of the law which now governs the obtaining of goods by false pretences, to cases where the false pretences consist in false statements, made, not necessarily directly to the person from whom the goods are immediately obtained, but for the purpose of obtaining credit on the part of the person making them in order that goods may be obtained. For instance, a person making a false statement of his affairs and furnishing that statement to a commercial agent, with a view to obtaining thereby credit among the business public, is made guilty of an offence by reason of his making that statement. The making of that statement is made an offence without it being necessary to proceed to prove that the goods were actually obtained by means of it. The amendment also makes it an offence for any person to procure goods on behalf of any person who has made such a false statement, knowing that statement to have been made, and obtaining goods on the strength of it.

Would that clause reach insurance agents making false representations or false statements as to the standing of an insurance company? It often happens that agents, such as insurance agents and machine agents, go into the country districts and make certain representations, and they are not reached 'exactly by the Criminal Code at present. Would they come under that clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I presume there might be a concrete case, where the statement made by an insurance agent with regard to the standing, and so forth, of the company he represented might perhaps bring him within the terms of this clause, or perhaps rather of the law as it now stands. I suppose he would obtain money in the shape of his commission by means of that false statement. What was in contemplation was not a case of that kind. What is in contemplation is the act of a man engaged in business who makes false statements as to the condition of his affairs. Such statements are usually furnished to agencies, to the banks and other people, and it may happen that although goods are not intended to be obtained from the person to whom the statement is directly furnished, the purpose is to obtain credit generally upon such false statements, and the object of the amendment is to make such false statements an offence.
Section 17 provides for the adoption by the Crown of marks for the identification of public property.
Section 18 has for its purpose the extension of the provisions in regard to protecting warehouses, shops and counting houses to cages or dens in which fur-bearing animals are kept. I understand that the industry of raising fur-bearing animals is assuming larger proportions, and it seems proper that the houses, or cages, in which they are kept, should be given the same protection as other buildings in which goods are kept.
Section 19 deals with the protection of letter boxes, and provides specially for the protection of Tural mail delivery boxes.

You are not afraid of
suffragettes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The next section is for the purpose of preventing the making or circulation of any coin or token which may be mistaken for, or may be intended to be taken for, any current coin.
Section 21 is to correct an error in the French version of section 594 of the Criminal Code.
Section 22 deals with the right of search in gaming houses and disorderly houses. The special change is with regard to the officer on whose information the magistrate has to issue a warrant. At present it is provided that the chief constable should lay the information. That has been found

very difficult of practical application, and the substantial amendment in this section extends the right to ask for a search warrant to the chief constable and his officers.
Section 23 makes it possible to arrest without warrant persons entering a military fortress when such arrest is asked for by the Militia Department.
Section 24 makes it possible to arrest without warrant persons reasonably suspected of offences under the sections which deal with what is called the white slave traffic. It has been found in a large number of cases that persons whom circumstances indicated to be clearly guilty have escaped by reason of the fact that it has been necessary to delay in order to procure a warrant to affect their arrest.
Would the minister go back to the previous section? I understand that it says that a man may be arrested without warrant who is found on a military property. To what extent does that go?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section is in amendment of section 646 of the Criminal Code. That section provides that any person may be arrested without a warrant who is found committing any of the offences mentioned, and then it goes on to enumerate a large number of sections of the criminal code. The purpose of this is to add to paragraph (a) of article 646 the following words:
Eighty-five and eighty-six, information illegally obtained or communicated.
Section 85 makes any person liable to prosecution whofor the purpose of wrongfully obtaining information enters or is in any part of a fortress, arsenal, factory, dockyard, camp, ship, office or other like place in Canada belonging to His Majesty, in which part he is not entitled to be, or when lawfully or unlawfully in any such place as aforesaid, either obtains any document, sketch, plan, model or knowledge of anything which he is not entitled to obtain, or takes without lawful authority any sketch or plan, or when outside any fortress, arsenal, factory, dockyard or camp in Canada, belonging to His Majesty, takes, or attempts to take, without authority given by op on behalf of His Majesty, any sketch or plan of that fortress, arsenal, factory, dockyard or camp;
The offences themselves already exist under the law as it stands and the purpose is to include violations of this section among the offences for which an arrest may be made without a warrant. The militia authorities consider this of importance to them for the protection of the military works throughout the country and above all for the effective prevention of the obtaining of information by persons who are not entitled to do so.
Mr. DOHERTY.
Does not that provision place pretty broad powers in the hands of a few military officers? I am afraid it is opening up a pretty wide door.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The power will be
slightly widened by this addition. There are numerous offences, very similar to these, in regard to which persons may be arrested without warrant. But I should be very glad to hear any observations that may be made upon the subject later on.
I would be afraid that if I went on the military grounds at the rifle ranges some sergeant might come along and simply put me under arrest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that
any sergeant, on the appearance of the hon. gentleman, would arest him on suspicion of having any dishonest purpose.

Does my hon.
friend the Minister of Justice remember the case on the Champs de Mars a few years ago when a sentry arrested a gentleman who was simply crossing the place on the occasion of a review.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would be very glad
to consider any possible effects of this suggested amendment later on. While I am proposing these amendments I certainly look to the House for assistance, advice and suggestions, and I shall be glad to have them. These are matters which nobody is interested in save with the view of improving the law and making it more effective while at the same time seeking not to do anything which will unduly interfere with the liberty of the subject. I shall be glad, when we come to the committee stage, to hear any suggestions that may be made and to give them every consideration.

Is there anything in
the Bill, or is it the intention of the Minister of Justice to propose any legislation, to make the penalties more stringent against persons engaged in the cocaine traffic which has been a plague in the large cities? Any number of people have been arrested both for selling and using cocaine. It is becoming a regular pest. My hon. friend from Montcalm (Mr. La-fortune), the Crown prosecutor in Montreal, states that the public is up in arms against the habit and the traffic. I would like to know if my hon. friend proposes to make the penalty more stringent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, this Bill does not propose to make the penalty more stringent. I have not received any representations to the effect that the present law does not provide a sufficient penalty. The matter was dealt with, I think, in the last session of the last Parliament and a law

providing what were regarded as fair penalties was enacted.

I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the matter. I follow the press pretty closely and it is apparent that this offence has become more general within the last few years. The number of the victims of cocaine and morphine has become simply appalling. I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the investigations which have been made into this question and I would urge him whether such legislation cannot be enacted as will prevent people from falling into the habit or engaging in the traffic. I remember that, in the city of Montreal last fall, the police authorities discovered two or three places where young men and young women were established, as they are in China and in some western cities on the coast, using opium. I saw that a man was arrested the otheT day, I think, in Ottawa, for selling a drug on the street. The drug was found in his hat. It is said that the traffic is going on in large cities. I am perhaps out of order because there is nothing on this subject contained in this Bill, but I simply wish to bring the matter to the attention of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
speak at the moment on the matter, but my hon. friend will recollect that, as I said, in that last session of the last Parliament, the tihen Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mackenzie King, caused to be passed some legislation which, I think, met with the approval of Parliament generally, for the purpose of getting at and suppressing the evil to which my hon. friend refers. I have not had it represented to me that that legislation was insufficient or ineffective. I shall be very glad to look into what the penalty is and to make inquiry amongst those charged with the administration of the law with a view to ascertaining whether there is need of doing something further in that regard. Then, as I said, section 24 gives the power to arrest without warrant persons reasonably suspected of offences under the provisions of the law in regard to the white slave traffic.

I would like to ask the
minister if the punishment provided for white slaves includes the lash?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In regard to a certain class of offences, whipping forms part of the punishment that may be imposed.
They have adopted that mode of punishment in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. The other provisions all have to do with matters of procedure and I do not think it is necessary
for me to go into detail with regard to them.

There is a very important point in connection with the matter of procedure to which I would draw the attention of the Minister of Justice. It has reference to the reading of depositions. At the preliminary examination witnesses for the prosecution are brought in and give their evidence, and their depositions may be afterwards read at the trial. But, supposing that the accused desires to have read the deposition of a witness who has died or who has gone away from the country, or who, for some other reason, is not present at the trial, he is precluded from having that deposition read, while the prosecution is permitted to have its depositions read. I think it is most important that some amendment in connection with this matter should be made to the law, and it would be well if it could be included in this Bill, because the present law deprives the defence of a great privilege. A man might be sent to the scaffold by reason of the fact that he has not the privilege of reading depositions at the trial.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is introducing the discussion of matters which are not included in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Among the sections
contained in the Bill is one modifying in some respects the provision in regard to the depositions that may be read at trials. While the proposed legislation does not permit depositions taken on behalf of the accused to be read, when we come to deal with the section, I shall be very glad to listen to, and meet if possible, any suggestion that my hon. friend may make.

May I inquire '
of the Minister of Justice whether he intends to bring in legislation concerning penitentiaries ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I do propose to
introduce legislation in regard to the salaries and wdges of penitentiary employees. I hope to introduce that Bill on Monday or Tuesday.
May I ask the minister if he intends to introduce any legislation for increasing the district and county court judges salaries this session ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to an increase in the salaries of the judges, I am very much afraid it will not be possible for us to deal with that matter this session. It has been discussed on a previous occasion. I pointed out some of the matters involved in connection with the question and their nature. The difficulty that arises in connection with this matter of judicial salaries largely results

from the different conditions that prevail in different provinces, not only from the point of view of the cost of living, but more particularly in regard to the legislation which prescribes the number of judges, their duties and their possible emoluments, which may be derived from other sources than their salaries. To deal with the matter in a manner which would be just to the judges in the different provinces and under these different conditions will be exceedingly difficult without cooperation on the part of the legislatures of certain of the provinces. It will not be the easiest task imaginable. These difficulties make it impossible that [DOT] we should hope to introduce at this session a measure which we could reasonably expect to have passed, because all of these differences in the conditions of judges will cause considerable discussion and produce differences of opinion with regard to any measure which would seek to deal with the subject.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. DOHERTY
years. No. A Bill similar to this one was ratified last year. There is no change,

On section 1-fruit marks:
Will the hon. minister give us some explanation of the Bill?

On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Agriculture), Bill No. 199, to amend the Inspection and Sale Act, was read the second time, and House went into commr. uuviui: lms Bill is a departure in principle from the Inspection and Sale Act as it stands at the present time. The Inspection and Sale Act makes provision for the inspecting and marking of fruit imported into Canada. There is a very radical principle contained in this Bill, and a very wide authority is taken by the Government in regard to it. The matter is one of such importance and affects the interests of a very large number of people so intimately that I take the position that if the Government have certain views in regard to the marking of imported fruit, those views should be stated in the statute,' and not expressed by the Governor in Council. It is quite possible, as my hon. friend knows, to administer the law under this section so as practically to prohibit the importation of fruit into Canada. I know that the principle of taking all authority into the hands of the Government is, of course, a well-established principle on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, but it is none the less objectionable from my point of view. I say that if the Government considers it proper-and I am not arguing that point-that there should be a new provision introduced into the Inspection and bale Act, providing for the marking of imported fruit, that provision should be statutory and not made by Order in Council.

I cannot agree that we are introducing a new principle in the proposed Bill, because in section 321 of the old Act there is a clause saying that no person shall sell or offer or expose or have in his possession for sale any fruit packed and so on. The only difficulty, which has been pointed out by the Justice Department, is that while we are operating under that section against all fruit, it should be made a little clearer, because in the main the Act was directed against fruit grown in this country. As to what the hon. member for Edmonton says with regard to the powers of the Governor in Council, I would point out that the original Act is amended by adding thereto section 320. That section lays down the

regulations in regard to the grades and the marking, and it is abundantly clear that this new section is simply incorporated into the old, and that the same method as to marking will be pursued. The onlyv desire is that we shall be able to deal with all fruit on the same basis.
Mr. CARVELL. Is it provided that packages containing fruit imported into Canada must be branded in a certain way, as directed by Order in Council. Can the Government prescribe what the marking shall be? Under the Inspection and Sale Act we have, of course, the right to prescribe how fruit exported from Canada shall be marked. We felt that we were suffering because the people were marking fruit as superior and sending it to the British and other markets. To meet that condition of affairs, what I considered to be a very rigid regulation was applied to prevent 'this illegal marking. But the present Bill seems to act entirely upon a different principle. If I import fruit into Canada, under this proposed legislation, it must be marked in a certain way. How is the man who puts up grapes in Spain-and we import hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of grapes from Spain each year-to know exactly what brand or mark must be placed upon the packages in which the grapes are shipped? When he puts up his fruit he expects to sell it over the world. Has he got to put on a special mark in order to reach the Canadian market? Is the Canadian consumer to be denied the right of buying grapes from Spain because the packer has not oomplied with all the requirements set out in the Canadian regulations? I am afraid that under the operation of this proposed legislation the price of fruit in Canada will be increased. If there is anything which should be made cheaper in Canada it is fruit. Eor oranges, bananas, apples, pears and peaches we are paying two prices in some parts of Canada. Under the operation of this Act it would seem that if a man desires to bring peaches * from the state of New York, unless the packages are branded in a certain way, be is liable to the application of these regulations. If, for instance, a dealer imports 100 boxes of peaches, and places them in his store, and if they are not branded according to regulations he may be told that he is liable to a fine of $50 if he sells them.
I may be submitting a very strong illustration, but it seems to me that that will be the 'logical result of the passage of this Bill. Many of these fruits we import from the United States, usually from Boston. This is made imperative by reason of the exorbitant freight rates which a dealer has to pay if he attempts to bring them from some portion of Canada, resulting in his Mr. BURRELL.
charging very high prices for the fruit. Supposing a dealer in my town or any other town in the Maritime provinces orders a shipment of grapes, peaches, pears or plums from Boston; they^ arrive by express, and he places them in his store. If they are not marked in a certain way, he is liable to a fine of $500. Surely that is not right. I believe this Bill is proposed for the very purpose of preventing our people from importing fruit from the United States, and of compelling them to buy from the home producers. It may be all very well for a few people in the Niagara peninsula, but it is bad for the consumers of Canada. I think we have enough protection on fruit now without giving it additional protection in this roundabout and disguised manner. If I am wrong, I would like the minister to correct me; if I am right, I think he should withdraw this Bill.

My hon. friend is subjecting himself to a good deal of unnecessary alarm. There is no great difference between this Bill and the old Act, which was placed on the statute-book by the previous Government. The old Act covered exactly what this does, but there was a weakness in it with regard to our power. Under this proposed legislation we do not intend to deal with such fruit as the hon. gentleman has mentioned; as a matter of fact, it is chiefly intended to apply to the apple trade. In regard to the grades and other matters dealt with by my predecessors after a con- 1 ference, no doubt, with all concerned, this Bill deals almost entirely with apples. There is not the slightest intention to touch such fruit as my hon. friend has mentioned, or interfere in any way with that trade. The sole object of the Bill is to make the old Act a little clearer by giving the Government ample power to provide such regulations as will put the imported apples exactly in the same position as the native-grown apples. It is true that the Act may be extended, to some extent, to pears and peaches and fruits put up in certain grades. We have been prosecuting, in behalf of every consumer in this country, scores and scores of apple-growers in Canada because they have not been packing honestly, and in doing that we feel that we should have the right, in regard to the same fruit, to prosecute anybody who sells fruit packed or branded in a dishonest manner.
I must say that the answer of my hon. friend hardly removes the suspicion I have in my mind with regard to this Bill.

My hon. friend is
very full of suspicion.

I may be, but I think
I am discussing this matter from the standpoint of the consumer of this country. We must assume that the jobber or retailer

buying fruit does not desire to buy an inferior product if he can help it. He is going to buy the best he can get, and if he buys it and brings it into this country, he is liable to a fine of $50 if he sells fruit which has not been branded according to the regulations. In this Bill the hon. minister is carrying out the well-defined principle of this Government-that of government by Order in Council and not by Parliament. The Government desires to get the same power with regard to fruit as with regard to the Highways and Agricultural Acts, the Naval Bill, and everything else. They say: give us the money; give us the power; we do not intend to exercise it in any unfair way; give us the power, and trust us. It has been said many times by members on this side of the House that individually we respect the gentlemen who are occupying the treasury benches, but why is it necessary to give them all these powers and take their word that they will not exercise them improperly? My hon. friend says this legislation is intended to protect the country regarding apples. I do not object to that, because we do not have to import apples into Canada. It is quite right and proper that the .producer of apples in Canada, over whom we have jurisdiction, should be compelled to label and mark his fruit properly, but we have not jurisdiction over the producers in Spain and California. If my hon. friend intends that this legislation shall apply only to apples, let him say so; if he intends that the legislation shall go further than that, let him say so. If he does say that it is intended to go further, I think this proposed legislation is an unwarranted interference with the rights of the people, who ought to have the right to buy their fruit in the cheapest market they can find.

Did the hon. minister
see a letter I wrote to his deputy some time ago in regard to the kind of packing in which the apples should be packed?
No.

I would like the hon.
minister to ask his deputy to let him see that communication, that he may look it over and advise me as to whether or not the regulations could be changed in accordance with my suggestion. I bring this matter up for the purpose of criticising not the minister's Bill, but the regulations of the department. I am free to admit that these regulations were made by the hon. gentleman's predecessors; I am not quite certain, however, that they were always correct, although they were as nearly so as they could be. As the matter is one of very considerable importance, I would like the hon. minister to look into it and let us have his views.
Is my hon. friend alluding to the regulations, or to the Act?
I am alluding more particularly to the regulations.
Section 325 of the old Act deals with the size of the package.
I was under the impression that the dimensions of the packages were fixed by the regulations, rather than by the Act.

I think it is by the statute.

On motion of Hon. W. T. White ' (Minister of Finance), House went into Committee to consider Bill No. 36, respecting Banks and Banking. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-short title:

I was not
able to follow the progress made in the Banking and Commerce Committee. Might I ask my hon. friend if the committee has made any serious changes in the Bill presented by him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No doubt my right hon. friend is aware that the Bill was very fully considered by the committee, that a great deal of evidence was taken and that the clauses were all under very full discussion. In a general way, I may say that the Bill has not been substantially modified from the form in which it was introduced to the House. A few changes of an important nature have been made and I shall briefly indicate them for the information of my right hon. friend. In the first place, my right hon. friend will recollect the clause providing for an audit of the chartered banks. To that provision of the Bill, the committee added the further provision that the auditors shall be chosen from a list of forty named and selected in the first instance by the general managers of the 'Chartered banks of Canada who are the members of the Chartered Bankers' Association. They are to be selected by them by ballot and their selection is subject to the veto of the Minister of Finance. From that rota the shareholders of the bank shall select auditors in accordance with the provisions which were in the Bill when brought originally before the House. A further provision has been made by the committee for the registration of the liens which the new Act authorizes banks to take upon threshed grain and cattle. Some slight modification has been made, although the law has not been altered, in the sec-

As I understand it, then, the modifications which have been made are not of a serious character? It seems to me that only two important changes have been made the first of which is in regard to the audit. I do not exactly understand why there should be such complicated machinery, but that will be explained, I suppose, when we come to the clause itself. Then, the other important change is that under the new provision in regard to the taking of liens on chattels and things of that kind, these securities have to be registered while other securities do not require to be. There is a difference between the two classes of securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not quite understand what my right hon. friend means.
I understand that by the new Act farmers may borrow on the security of grain and things of that kind, and that these pledges have to be registered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a change made
by the committee.

Whereas
other pledges continue to be non-registered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance if he proposes following the course that was pursued in the committee, that is to go through the non-contentious clauses first and then take up those in regard to which there may be some difference of opinion. I think it will be found that Mr. WHITE (Leeds)
there are still a number of sections which were apparently disposed of in the committee that will be more fully considered here. There were some proposed amendments that were steam-rollered out of existence in the committee and I think it would be well for the House to consider these proposed amendments in Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it is thought advisable that any particular clause should stand I would be very glad to allow it to stand, but I think it would be inadvisable to go over each one of them three times because it would take up a good deal of the time of the House. I think we will be able to make very good progress and at the same time to preserve to my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson), or any other hon. member, the right to defer a section for further consideration.
On section 2-definitions; Association.
Is this the first recognition of the Canadian Bankers' Association in the Bank Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The Canadian Bankers' Association is an incorporated body and this definition is for the purposes of the present Act, especially the selection of an auditor.
Is the Canadian Bankers' 'Association specifically recognized in the existing Bank Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Why are hogs excluded from the definition of ' cattle ' on which a bill of sale can be given? There is nothing in the Bill to draw the distinction between a rancher and a farmer, and I am satisfied that will lead to considerable trouble, because, for example, a man might be both a rancher and a farmer and who will draw the distinction. Then, a farmer can pledge or hypothecate his cattle which includes everything except hogs. Where is the logic in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The privilege of making a loan by way of lien was extended to meet especially the case of the West, and is particularly of advantage to the western farmer in regard to his threshed grain. The committee was of opinion it would not be wise to extend the privilege of giving a lien to farmers generally upon cattle or live stock. In the present Bank Act, manufacturers engaged in wholesale business are permitted to give a lien upon their products, but the retailer is not, the wholesale idea being the principle adopted. In the West the banks have been in the habit of taking a lien upon the cattle of ranchers, who, so to speak, raise animals wholesale. It is not the intention of the commission that

liens should be extended to farmers generally throughout the country, upon their cattle, sheep or hogs. It was thought that the animals mentioned would include all these raised by ranchers, and hogs have been omitted. The legislation is exceptional and designed to meet the conditions in the West, although in terms, of course, it is general.

The minister has correctly stated the intention of the committee, and personally I could see no object in the legislation until the change was made by which the lien should be registered. Once the committee decided that, the legislation is proper enough. I do not see why a farmer should not be able to go to a bank and borrow money on his nogs as well as on his cattle, so long as the lien is properly registered. Unless the minister says he is opposed to this policy and that he was forced into adopting it by the insistence of the member for Brandon and others, and having adopted it, he wished to confine the principle as narrowly as possible, I cannot see any logic in it. To my mind, what is the most valuable asset on which a farmer can raise money has been omitted. The hog is ready for sale at six months, and any other animal takes perhaps three years to fit for market. In my opinion the hog is the one item above all others upon which a farmer ought be allowed to obtain an advance from the bank.
The farmer has no right under this Act; it is the rancher.
Yes, I know, but there will be a lot of trouble in drawing a distinction between a farmer and a rancher.
The courts have always had to draw that distinction.

There are many in the
Maritime provinces who have three hundred or four hundred acres of land; two hundred acres would be a ranch with cattle and horses, and the balance would be cultivated and hogs would be raised. What is there in this Act which will help the court to interpret whether that man is a farmer or a rancher. The minister may have the distinction in his mind, but it is what the courts will decide that will rule. If the minister says he only did this as a matter of special favour to the West, and based on that principle the eastern farmer was out out, then there may be some logic in it.
Mr. MEIG-HEN:	The necessity for the
courts drawing a distinction between a rancher and a farmer has existed under the old Act, and the difficulty is no greater now than before. I have had suits in
which the courts drew the distinction as a matter of inference from the facts. In the case of a man who had a pledge to the bank, the court ascertained the business he was in in relation to cattle, and the proportion of that business as related to that of others in the neighbourhood, and from these facts they decided whether or, not he was a rancher or a farmer. It was not an easy task. All I want to say is that the courts are now loaded with no greater responsibilities or difficulties than they, were under the old Act. Previously a rancher was able to borrow money on his cattle. He is able to do so now legally. Previously a farmer was not able to do so. He is not able to do so now.

It is no answer to say that, because it was in the old Act, it should he put in this one. The object of this legislation is to remedy dififtculties that exist. What my hon. friend states only emphasizes the point I made. This distinction ought not to be drawn. If you give to one man the right to borrow money on his cattle, you ought to give it to every man. The fact tnat my hon. friend has had law suits in regard to the matter, while it might be of advantage to him, I think is evidence that this distinction should not be drawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hope to meet the objection of my hon. friend because I believe he and I see substantially eye to eye, as to the inadvisability of extending the principle of the lien to individuals, whether farmers or retailers. The principle, which has underlain the Bank Act since the original legislation was brought in, has been that the banks should make loans on personal security; that they should look to the individual, whether a farmer or a retailer, as their principal security, and that they should not engage in the business of making loans upon chattel mortgages. I believe that is a sound banking principle. The first invasion of that principle took place in the revision of the Bank Act in 1891, when the right of lien was given to the wholesale manufacturer, by reason of his raw material being worked up through several processes and the desirability of his being able to pay cash. The idea was that wholesalers should have it and that retailers should not. That has been the principle of the Act until this revision. I do not believe it is in the interest of the public or of the banks that farmers or retailers or individuals, speaking generally, should have the privilege of going to a bank and borrowing money upon chattel mortgages. I should not like to see the banks engaged in chattel mortgage business. I do not believe my hon. friend would. He is aware of the circumstances under which we introduced this legislation,



namely: in order to provide for liens upon threshed grain. The committee, after giving that matter very full consideration, and having regard to the peculiar situation in the West in regard to the storage of grain and lack of transportation facilities came to the conclusion that such loans should be permitted. We are not giving to the farmer the right to borrow by way of lien upon his cattle, sheep or other animals. We are only giving that right to the rancher, who in a sense is a wholesaler. My hon. friend knows how difficult it is to define terms. In 1891 they tried to define the word ' wholesale,' and they failed. They came to the conclusion that the definition would have to be left to the decision of the courts, if necessary. Once you attempt to define, you only confuse. The wholesale idea is contained in the word ' rancher,' a man who is engaged in the raising of cattle or sheep or other animals upon a large scale. Mv hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has pointed out that the matter has had to be dealt with by the courts even under the present Act,

I am very much of the opinion of the minister. The only difficulty is that we are opening the door for litigation. We should either refuse to extend the principle/or make it so broad that there will be no question in the matter. If the principle is extended so that a man can borrow money on horses or cattle, there is no reason why he should not have the right to borrow money on hogs. If you give to one man the right to borrow money on horses or cattle or hogs, you ought to give that right to every man in Canada. That is my point. My hon. friend is only creating a condition of affairs which will be fruitful of litigation. I will give an illustration. I have a business proposition under way now by which another gentleman and myself intend to go into the business of sheep raising. We are going to run a farm for sheep alone. We shall not have a thousand acres of land, and we are going to raise hay and other grain with which to feed the sheep. We do not expect to sell a pound of hay or grain or anything else on the farm except sheep. Will the hon. minister tell me whether we shall be farmers or ranchers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I look upon my hon.
friend as a legislator of renown, so I am not going to call him either a rancher or a farmer.
If we do not adopt this clause, it means that ranchers will be deprived of the privilege of borrowing upon their cattle or other animals. The baulks in the West today take liens upon the cattle of ranchers. Some doubt has been expressed upon that point by a decision in the Alberta courts, Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
and it was thought advisable that it should be cleared up, because we believe it to be very much in the interest of the public that men engaged in cattle raising in a wholesale way should have the privilege which they have across the line, of borrowing upon their cattle and other animals. It was to make that certain that this clause was introduced. We have not gone the length of extending the privilege to the farmers. The committee, after hearing all the evidence on that point, thought that that should not be done. I think my hon. friend has the same view. There may be something in what he says as to the possibility of litigation.

We are now on the interpretation clauses, and the minister has informed the committee that there is a difference in treatment between the ranchers and the farmers in regard to identical articles. It strikes me that there should be an interpretation of the words 'farmer' and 'rancher,' if their is to be a fair understanding of how far the Bill is applicable to each class. I represent a constituency that includes a very large portion of the western provinces. It is a district in which the rearing of live stock is the principal occupation of farmers; it is a mixed farming country. As regards live stock, hog rearing is the most important industry in that section of the country. That condition prevails in the two adjoining constituencies. I did not attend the Banking and Commerce Committee; but I would have supposed, according to this Bill, that the farmers in that part of the country would have the same privilege, if it is a privilege, of borrowing against their cattle, horses and sheep, although not against their hogs, as the people in any other part of the West would have. From what the hon. minister says, I am compelled to understand that that very large area of the West is absolutely cut out of any benefit there may be in the provision, but the Bill does not say so. I think that in the interpretation clause there should be a specific statement of how far these provisions are applicable so that the people in that part of the country would not be under any misunderstanding; if they are not to get any benefit from this Act they ougnt to know it and it ought to be so stated on the face of the Act. I do not know why the distinction that my hon. friend speaks of should be drawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recognize that there are certain terms that cannot very well be further defined. Such words as gold and silver for instances cannot very well be further defined. There has been a judicial decision in which a rancher has been distinguished from a farmer. My idea is that the rancher is a man engaged

more particlarly in the industry of raising cattle or sheep or horses on a large scale, that the wholesale idea is embodied. I think it would be anything but good legislation and it would not be of advantage to the small farmer to permit the banks to take chattel mortgages practically on a horse or two, so as to become chattel mortgagees on farmers all over the country. That would not be a good banking principle. What we are trying to do is to build up the western cattle raising, sheep raising and horse raising industries, but we have not been willing to go to the length suggested and I think the evidence all shows that it would be inadvisable to give to farmers all over the country the privilege of mortgaging by way of secret lien or chattel mortgage on live stock.

The provision we are now discussing is supposed to be for the benefit of the western country, but it is not applicable to a very large section of country represented by myself and the members from the adjoining constituencies and, I think, my hon. friend from Prince Albert. The farmers in my constituency have always been engaged in mixed farming. No one ever goes into the western country without telling the people to go into mixed farming, but there is no encouragement to mixed farming under this Act. As to the difference between the wholesaler and retailer, there is no more difference between the large rancher and the small raiser of cattle, sheep or hogs, than there is between the man who raises five hundred bushels of wheat and the man who raises five thousand. As long as the lien is registered it seems to me the conflicting interests that might arise are sufficiently and fully protected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The evidence before us
shows conclusively that any farmer engaged in mixed farming would be able to get bank accommodation without giving a lien and there is this difference between the cases of threshed grain and cattle, that the question of transportation and storage of grain in the West pending marketing is a very serious one. That constitutes the difference between the case of the farmer with five thousand or ten thousand bushels of grain and the farmer who has live stock which, as my hon. friend has said, can be marketed at Edmonton or some other place where they have packing plants.
I observe that hogs are left out of the definition of animals. Is that why pease are left out of the definition of grain ? I do not know why pease should be left out.

Would it not be possible to insert the word ' hogs ' in the section in order that it should apply in the same way as to the wholesale ranchers?""I
quite appreciate what my hon. friend from Edmonton has said in regard to small farmers who raise a small number of hogs, but still, even if the minister did not accede to the suggestion made by that hon. member, if the word ' hogs ' were inserted it could be made applicable to the rancher who raises hogs. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that there are no hog ranchers in the West as there are cattle ranchers. I would be glad to be corrected if I am misinformed on that. I did not understand that hogs were raised in the West as cattle and sheep are.

No, they are not raised as cattle and sheep are. In some oases they do go into a certain amount of wholesale raising of hogs. In my constituency to such an extent are the people going into mixed farming and the raising of cattle on a small scale, and sheep and hogs, that local capital has gone into the erection of an abattoir on a fairly large scale and it is desirable that advantages should be given to hog raisers under the Banking Act. I think it would encourage that industry if the word ' hogs ' were inserted there, confining it to the wholesale ranchers if you like; it would not destroy the principle referred to by the minister.

I think that to extend the privileges of the banks to take liens on hogs would not have very much effect. I doubt very much whether the banks of Canada would take liens upon hogs. They might advance money and take liens on stock, horses and cattle, something which could be identified and brought in and realized on; but as hogs have only a few months' growth and as it is impossible to identify them, it would be difficult for the banker to bring them in and realize upon them. Where would you stop ? They might demand that the banks should have the liberty to lend on hens, chickens, &c.
Hear, hear; and ducks.

You must draw the line somewhere. To my mind the man raising grain can borrow enough under this Act to carry him along, without having to put a lien also on the stock he may be raising as an ordinary farmer. I am doubtful if there would be any particular advantage to the man raising hogs, because I do not believe any bankers would grant a lien on hogs.

I asked a number of
farmers about this and I know the farmers would like to have the privilege extended. If it was done for the farmers I know they would be very grateful.

As I understand the amendments to section 88 are based on two prin-

ciples. The bank may lend to a farmer upon the security of his threshed grain upon the farm. The reason for that is that grain is a most easily realizable security and the farmer in the West usually raises liis grain for immediate sale and it may be that he can only realize at a time when it is disadvantageous for him to do so. The purpose of this amendment is to give him the liberty to raise money from the bank without incurring much expense on the most soluble security that the farmer has, his threshed grain. The second principle is that a bank may lend money to a rancher upon the security of his cattle. The rancher is in principle in the same position as the wholesale manufacturer mentioned in the following sub-section. He raises money on his ranch animals. They are raised for the purpose of sale, and as soon as they become saleable they are sold, they are not raised for the purpose of keeping them on the farm for ordinary farming purposes. The hogs are usually raised in small numbers and they are not raised to any extent exclusively or in wholesale quantities upon ranches. Therefore it seems to me that it is better to leave the clause just as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would prefer to have the interpretation clause passed on the understanding that if we desire to make any changes .subsequently such changes can be made.

Some interpretation
should be put upon the word ' wholesale.' Under! seiction 83 the hanks may lend monev to a wholesale shipper of products of the sea. The words * purchaser, shipper or dealer ' in the Act are limited by the word ' wholesale.' In regard to the distinction drawn in sub-section 2 of section 88:
The bank may lend money to a farmer upon the security of his threshed grain grown upon the farm.
And in sub-section 3:
The bank may lend money to a rancher upon the security of hiB cattle.
I would like to point out that where I live the terms 'rancher' and 'farmer' are interchangeable. The man who is a farmer or a rancher as the case may be, raises cattle or horses or sheep, and certainly hogs and grain. I feel myself put in a very peculiar position if the interpretation of this Act remains as it is. I go back to my constituency, my constituents have access to the statute, and they find that certain privileges are set out on the face of the statute as being available to them, and yet I shall be compelled to tell them that, although available to them on the face of the statute, as a matter of fact, they are not available to them. It is a very unpleasant position for a representative of the people to be placed in, and I will not be alone in that position. I think that in the interpretation clause there should be some setting forth of the intention of the Government, whatever it may be, so that there shall be no misunderstanding on the part of the people as to how far the Act goes.
Mr. SHARPE (North Ontario:	Had the
committee extended the privilege of these loans to the farmer, I could understand the interpretation being made to include hogs, but it is confined to ranchers, as the minister has stated, and the committee were of the opinion that there were only cattle, horse and sheep ranches and not hog ranches in the West. It is news to members in the East to learn that there are ranches devoted exclusively to the raising of hogs. If such were the case there would be some reason in insisting upon the word ' hogs ' being inserted in the definition; otherwise I cannot see the force of my hon. friend's objection.

My hon. friend's point is not well taken. If he looks at section 88 he will see that the bank may lend money to the farmer upon his threshed grain, and

to the rancher upon the security of his cattle. Now, the people where I live have cattle and grain, and they are'called, interchangeably, ranchers and farmers because they are engaged in mixed farming. I would have supposed on the face of the Act that the man who has a bunch of steers in the Edmonton district, and who raised wheat as well, could raise money on his horses as well as on his wheat, but I am told by the minister that he cannot. I am not quarrelling with the minister, or with the committee, about that. They have adopted a certain principle. I think it is wrong, but let it be as they have decided. What I ask is that they shall show in the Bill what they intend so that it will convey to the minds of the people the exact facts.

As I understand it, in the general acceptation of the word, a rancher is one who is raising stock in wholesale or large quantities, and not a person engaged in mixed farming. I think that the people in the East, and in the province of Manitoba, whatever they may do in Alberta, consider a rancher to be not a mixed farmer, but one who is raising live stock almost exclusively. If the principle were changed, and instead of the word ' rancher ' the word ' farmer ' was inserted to allow the bank to lend money to the farmer on the security of his 'cattle, you would get into the class of small loans on varying securities, securities that are not immediately realizable. The Act generally relates to wholesale producers and wholesale manufacturers, and the security given is of the soluble class. That would not be so if we inserted the word ' farmer ' for * rancher,' because the advances that are ordinarily made to a farmer are secured by chattel mortgage. That would not be according to the principle of the Act. There is a difference in respect to threshed grain by reason of the fact, which I have already pointed out, that grain is readily marketable. If a banker wishes to realize on his security, he can immediately do so, because the grain is almost as good as gold and is a staple article which can find a ready market. Therefore, as I understand, the committee came to the conclusion to call the individual in one case ' farmer ' and in the other case * rancher.'

My hon. friend has stepped a little aside from the point. I was pointing out the desirability of defining what the Banking and Commerce Committee or the Government or the minister desire to convey when they debar the man who has wheat as well as horses from raising money on his horses, while they allow him To raise it on his wheat. I am asking that they shall show their intention on the face of the Bill, that is all. The contention that there is better security to the
bank on wheat than on horses, cattle, or hogs, is not well founded. My hon. friend knows that. He knows perfectly well that if it is a question of security to the bank, the cattle or the hogs, and especially the hogs, are better security than the wheat. My hon. friend says we must consider the wholesaler. Under the interpretation of this Act the man whose total wealth is represented by a bunch of thirty or forty cattle can get money under the provisions of this Act. A man who has the same number of horned stock but who has an equal number of horses, we will say, a hundred hogs and five thousand bushels of grain, could not secure the same money on his horned stock. This is such a palpable absurdity that I cannot understand the minister wanting it to pass. If he says that it is difficult to make the interpretation, all I have to say is that he occupies his position for the purpose of meeting and overcoming difficulties and he should not put legislation on the statute-book which is so absurdly discriminatory and which is discriminatory without reason or purpose.

What would be the
average value of marketable steers in the West on the ranch?
I could not answer that, because the price has varied very greatly, but at the moment I think that a good three year old steer will cost about $70.

The reason I ask the
question is that it has never appeared clear to me why there should be discrimination between a rancher who owns cattle and a farmer who owns cattle. There are any number of farmers, especially in the dairying districts of eastern Ontario and western Quebec, whose dairy cattle will provide a better security than the rancher's cattle. Why they should be deprived of the right thai is possessed by the ranchers is something that has never been clear to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not to go over the ground that has already been covered, I may say that the committee was of opinion that the farmer engaged in mixed farming, not only in the West but throughout Canada, should not be permitted to give a lien upon his live stock or chattel property to the bank. That has Deen the attitude of all legislation up to date in regard to the matter and it has been discussed very frequently in this House. We desire to give the man in the West, and elsewhere in Canada, who is engaged in the wholesale raising of cattle the privilege of securing a loan on the security of the live stock which he is engaged in raising. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), as I take it, thinks it possible to define the term. That occurred to us, but we have been unable to find a satisfactory definition for the word ' rancher.' There are a num-

ber of matters of this kind that cannot be defined without really adding to confusion. The word ' wholesale ' has not been defined in the Act and cannot be defined. It is better to leave it exactly as it is. We are engaged in considering section 2 in which the word ' rancher ' does not appear. But, it does appear in section 88, and when we come to section 88 we can discuss further this question to which my hon. friend has now drawn our attention and if it is found possible in the meantime to define the word ' rancher ' then I shall ask the committee to be allowed to insert in the interpretation clause the definition which may be agreed upon. I am not very hopeful of being able to do it. It is a very difficult matter, but, as my hon. friend says, it is the duty of the Government to overcome difficulties if it is at all possible to do it. It has not been found possible in the past to define the word ' wholesale ' and no untoward results have followed from it. There has not been much difficulty on the part of the commercial community in obtaining these liens, and it has been done without any very great loss or inconvenience. I would suggest that we pass section 2 now, subject to this, that if we find it necessary to change the interpretation clause of the Bill we may reopen it for that purpose.

I wish always to facilitate progress and I do not wish to seem to be too persistent, but this is a case in which there is a palpable and serious discrimination against the part of the country which I represent, and for that reason, while I do not intend to protest any longer, I am unable to agree that this section defining the word 1 cattle ' should be passed at this time.
