On section 43-conditions for transfer of shares:

We are entitled to explanation why clause (d) of this section is retained in the Act. I may be told it has been in the Bank Act for years, but we are now trying to make a better Act than we have had heretofore. I can, for example, buy one share of bank stock- that is about the size of my finances-and after I pay my $100 I get a certificate for the share and I suppose I own it, but I go to the bank to have the transfer made to me and I am told that the previous owner Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
of the share owed the bank fifty dollars and the bank refuses to transfer the shares to me. I know a case in the province of New Brunswick within the last year, in which a man, who is good for anything he might owe, assigned $20,000 worth of bank stock as security for a loan, and when that stock was taken to the bank to be transferred, the bank would not accept it because the previous owner owed the bank that money. That is unreasonable. This provision seems incompatible with the provisions of sections 45 and 46. Suppose under section 1 there is a public auction of bank shares and a man buys them in good faith at the market value, he goes to the transfer office and he is told: 'You cannot get the transfer because the original owner owes us money; true, we have security by an endorsed note, but we are a little afraid of the endorser; true, you bought them in. good faith at public auction and true you did not know we had a claim against the previous owner of the shares, but we will exercise the right which the law gives us and we will refuse to transfer.' In that case, the man who bought these shares in good faith at public auction finds he is gold-bricked. If I have $100 of bank stock it ought to be mine and if I become bankrupt the bank would not be entitled to a first lien on that to the exclusion of all my other creditors. It is an unfair, unreasonable, and unjust preference which the banks of this country have over and above the rights of all other creditors. It is nothing short of legal fraud on other creditors. I give notice that I shall test the opinion of the committee on this section, at whatever time is most convenient to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend was present at the committee when the evidence with respect to this section was given. I did have the same opinion as my hon. friend.
Did the bank managers convert you?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the evidence convinced the committee. This is known as the bank's lien upon its own shares as against the shareholder who is indebted to it. The hon. gentleman knows that the certificate the shareholder gets as to his holding of bank stock is not a scrip certificate with a power of attorney in blank upon the back which passes from hand to hand the same as in the case of other stock. The transfer of a bank share is made by the holder of the share giving a power of attorney to the broker or other person to transfer, and he goes to the bank and makes the transfer on the books from the seller to the buyer. The shares are not paid for until that is completed, in other words, until the legal title in them is vested in the seller or the lender as the case may be. The case

is therefore different from that of hypothecating or selling shares evidenced by scrip stock certificates which pass from hand to hand, and by estoppel give title. Therefore in the first case the loan has not been made until the shares have been actually transferred into the name of the lender, and in the second place the money would not be paid until the shares were transferred into the name of the purchaser. That is the usual course. It has never been brought to my attention that there have been abuses of this clause to the prejudice of lenders or purchasers in good faith. Now, on the fact of it, I admit this is an anomaly. In the case of incorporated companies there is no such lien, nor do I know of any other case in which the lien exists. When the matter was before the committee, we had a great deal of evidence along this line, which convinced the committee that it would probably be wise to let this lien stand, anomalous as it appears. The reason is this: the banks are not allowed to lend upon their own shares or upon the shares of other banks. Partly on account of the double liability and for other reasons, there is not a great deal of money seeking investment in bank shares; and it is desirable that that form of investment should be encouraged, in the interest not only of the banks, but of the country generally. It was pointed out, for example, that a holder of bank shares might desire to obtain a loan from a bank; but, by reason of the fact that banks are prohibited from loaning money on bank shares, he cannot get a loan upon his shares. If he cannot get it from private individuals or private or trust companies, he must sell his bank shares upon a very depressed market. The evidence given along that line convinced the committee that it would be in the interest of investors in bank shares and consequently in the interest of the community, in order that investment in bank shares might be promoted, if this clause were allowed to stand. Personally, I have an open mind on the matter. If, after hearing this explanation, my hon. friend or any other hon. gentleman desires this clause to stand so that he may move an amendment to strike it out, I shall be very glad indeed to allow it to stand. The argument which I have given was really the argument which convinced the committee.

My hon. friend states
he has an open mind. I fear he has been mesmerized by the bank magnates, just as other gentlemen of the committee have been. As I understand his explanation, it means that, because banks do not issue scrip certificates the same as other incorporated companies do, they should be allowed to take advantage of a wrong in order to possess a right which the holder of shares in an ordinary joint stock company does not hold. He says that the banks do not issue a certificate in the form of a scrip certificate; that they only issue a receipt. That is true. I would say: Go back to the beginning and make the banks issue a certificate.
How would you deal with the double liability?

The man who is on
record in the banks as holding the certificate is the man who pays the double liability.

Would you make the
banks issue certificates as ordinary companies do?

I am trying to answer
my hon. friend. I would make the banks issue a certificate just the same as is done in a joint stock company. I would make the man in whose name the certificate stands liable for the double liability. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance says that, because the banks issue receipts for money and not certificates, they should be allowed to take advantage of this and to have a lien upon their stock, a right which no other companies have.

Mr. SPEAKER.
Ho-'-se again went into Committee on Bill No. 36, respecting Banks and Banking.- (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

When the committee
rose I was pointing out to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that I was unable to follow his line of argument. It has been said that because the banks issue a receipt and not a stock certificate, they should be allowed to treat this receipt in a different manner from that in which the stock certificate of any incorporated company is treated. My hon. friend also said that as the bank cannot loan money on its own certificate or on the certificate of any incorporated company, in times of stringency the -man who owns a stock certificate and nothing else would not be in a position to obtain advances, because that, being his only security, could not be used in the bank. If my hon. friend had followed that line of reasoning as fax as he had intended, I presume the next step would have been to admit that a man could go to a bank and obtain money on his own responsibility, without any security whatever, simply because the bank knew that he had a hidden secret lien upon a certain amount of bank stock. On account of that hidden lien, the bank would make an advance to that party without any other security whatever, although the man himself might be financially worthless, except for the few dollars of bank stock he held. I will admit that that is an advantage to the man who happens to own bank stock, but I want my hon. friend to follow this same individual a little further. We will say that this business man is absolutely bankrupt, except in his ownership of the bank stock which he holds. He goes to the bank and they surreptitiously loan him on his own responsibility, practically the full value of that stock, because they know that the stock is in his name and that he cannot put in any other man's name without their consent. But the same man might go to his friend, neighbour or solicitor and say: I have got so many shares of certain bank stock, worth so much a share, and I would; like to get an advance on them. The person to whom he applies makes the advance, and takes the certificate as collateral security. In due course the loan is not paid, and the person who has made it takes the certificate to the bank and asks to have it transferred. But the bank officials say: No; we have a lien against that certificate. See the position in which you have placed the third party. The whole question hinges upon the matter of the registration of farmers' notes and liens, which was the subject of a heated discussion when the matter was before the committee. It is a bad principle; you have

no right to allow the bank to loan money on cattle, horses, grain, sheep or anything else, unless it is put on record, so that the public may be aware of the fact. Following the same line of argument, you have no right to allow the bank tp loan money on its own stock unless the public know something about it. If you do, you are giving to the hank and to the owner of stock a right which you do not give to the ordinary public, and you are giving them a chance to be dishonest if they so desire. I do not say that this privilege has been very much abused, but I have given the hon. minister an illustration to -show that it has been abused. I do not think anybody suffered very much, because fortunately the parties we-e perfectly solvent, and they had no difficulty in arranging the matter satisfactorily. I am only pointing out to my hon. friend what may happen if this clause is retained in the Bank Act. The hon. minister has submitted the explanation made to him by the bankers, which apparently converted him, but I can only say that in offering this explanation he "has not succeeded in converting me.

I did not have the
advantage of being associated with the Banking and Commerce Committee when this matter was discussed, but I have in past years given the matter a great deal of attention, and in this clause I fail to -see any injustice. The hon. member for Car-leton (Mr. Carvell) eliminated from his argument the well-known principle that in this country a man is supposed to know the law. He mentioned as an illustration the case of a man who loaned money on a bank certificate, but if that man had known the law he would not have suffered. He should have known that the share could cnly be transferred subject to the lien held on it by the bank or at least the bank s consent. His own carelessness and recklessness are to blame if he lends money upon that certificate without making inquiries from the bank.
Mr. CARVELL. Does my hen. friend think that that is reasonable from a business standpoint?
Wa have had this law since Confederation, and I do not think that a man who encounters difficulties bv lending money carelessly and recklessly is suffering an injustice.

My hon. friend will admit that it is one of the cardinal principles of banking that the private affairs of a customer shall not be disclosed. If I went to the bank and inquired whether the hon. member for Lincoln had obtained a loan, does the hon. gentleman think they would tell me?

The hon. gentleman
means that the confidential relations between a customer or stockholder and the banker would prevent that information being given. Even so, the man should still be on his guard and get the bank's consent. Using the illustration of my hon. friend, the gentleman in question should find out whether the hon. member for Lincoln was indebted to the bank to the extent of an amount which could be set off against his share. He should say: What sort of a man is this; is he likely to be a man who would do this? Supposing my hon. friend were in some business, and I bought a share in the business, would my hon. friend say it would be unfair, if I became insolvent, that he should be allowed to set off against my -share in the business any amount he had loaned me because I had that share in the business? Certainly he would be allowed to do so. My creditors could only get what was coming to me over and above what my hon. friend was entitled to take out of it. If I bought a tenth share of any business owned by some other man, a dry goods store or a sheep ranch, and because I had that interest in that business the owner allowed me to get some money from him, on my insolvency, my assignee or the sheriff could only force that other man to pay what was owing by virtue of a settlement of accounts between us and because the men in question here has a share in that bank or an interest in any bank, whatever it may be, surely it is no injustice that that bank should say: You have an interest in the bank, you owe us some money and the one should be set off against the other. I could never see any unfairness because among other people where the banks are not concerned the .thing would work out in the same way on the insolvency of the man who had the share in the other business.

The
representatives of the bank expressed themselves as indifferent whether this clause was left in or out. Jhey did not very forcibly defend it. Their reasons against the elimination of the clause was that it might discourage the purchase of bank shares. That might be said about any clause of the Bank Act that is in the interest of the bank. I quite agree with what the hon. member for Carleton said in regard to it being undesirable from many points of view. In the first place it makes the Bank Act the medium for collecting debts to the bank from the shareholders. The present clause allows the bank to lend practically on their own shares and my opinion is that that is not desirable legislation. There is no such provision in the company law and as the bank managers did not defend it I think it would be in the

interest of proper and good legislation to have this clause eliminated.

I am in favour of eliminating what I would call a preference that is sui generis with regard to the business world. I see no reason why the hanks should be placed in a preferential position as against all other concerns.

I would suggest that the
clause be allowed to stand. The arguments presented have been weighty, the committee came to this conclusion having regard to the interest of the shareholders rather than the interest of the bank. I have an open mind in the matter and at first was strongly in favour of striking it out

Is not the principle
involved in this sub-section involved in section 77 ?

In the oase of insolvency of a bank we find that some shares have been transferred, as in the case of the Bank of St. John and St. Hyaeinthe to insolvent people, or charitable institutions. Is there anything in the law Which would give power to the directors to refuse a transferee who was not in good financial standing, so that in the case of a bank failing the shares would not be held by people against whom the double liability could not be enforced? Section 61-issue and circulation of notes:

There are
new provisions in this section. Will the minister explain them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter of note circulation of banks was given very full consideration in the committee. In a word, the circulation privileges under the present Bank Act, both ordinary and emergency, have been continued in the present Bill, and one further provision has been added, that in addition to the ordinary power to issue up to the amount of their fully paid-up capital, and power of emergency circulation during the crop periods, the banks may issue an amount of notes equivalent to the gold deposited by them in a central gold reserve, for the establishment of what provision is made in this section. A great deal of evidence was given before this committee, and I think there was no dissent by any banker, or by anyone else, so far as I heard from the

advisability of the provision herein made. In the result, the banks will deposit gold in this central gold reserve, and up to the. amount of that deposit they may issue their notes when required for the carrying on of their- business, but not exceeding the amount so deposited.

Is this done without
Government supervision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have provided in the
Bill that the Government shall appoint one of the trustees, and the Bankers Association the two others, and that the gold reserve shall be inspected periodically by the Finance Department.
Does that mean that the Government will have knowledge from day to day of the amount of gold and of the amount of notes issued for circulation against that gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say from day to day, except that the Government's trustee would have knowledge, and the Government would have knowledge through their trustee. Books, of course, showing precisely the position would have to be kept by the trustees. It is very well safeguarded along the lines which I think my hon. friend has in mind. In addition there is an inspection by the Finance Department provided.
This is a provision to enable banks to issue increased circulation without their assets being increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In substance, I think my
hon. friend is correct, but I would rather put it this way. A bank, let us say, has today two million dollars of gold. Of course it can pay that over its counter, but the public do not take gold. The gold is not in general circulation, so the bank can go to the office of the Receiver General and obtain Dominion notes to circulate, these being at its disposal. We are providing that the bank may deposit a large amount of gold in this central reserve which can be issued up to the amount of that gold but not beyond it. It makes a more flexible situation. Under the present Act the bankers for fear of finding that they have come to the limit, or close to the limit, of their circulation stop. They do not go to the very apex of their circulation, because they are operating over a very large field, and they are afraid to exceed the circulation. If a bank had, say, $5,000,000 in gold, lodged in the central reserve, it would never have any fear. The result will be more circulation available for the needs of the country. It was clearly shown before the committee that one of the needs of the country was additional circulation, especially at particular periods of the year, to meet the requirements of commerce and trade.

I just want to fix the point thoroughly that this provision is for the purpose of increasing the circulation of bank notes, without placing any charge upon the banks, and without any increased assets or any increased gold to meet these notes. However desirable it may be to have increased circulation, it is even more desirable that there should be an adequate amount of gold behind that circulation. The arrangement up to the present time has been such that in my opinion we have never had too much gold behind our circulation, certainly not too much to meet times of stress and difficulty, which must always be considered. We are now preparing to increase our circulation, without increasing the gold behind the circulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The present Act does not require that a certain percentage of gold shall be kept; that is in the discretion of the bank. There has been no provision in the Bank Act that they must keep a certain percentage of gold although, as a matter of fact, the practice of bankers has always been to keep a certain amount of gold. Under the present legislation the banks go to the office of the Receiver General, get Dominion notes and circulate those. We are providing that they may deposit gold and issue their own notes. They make no money out of that. The only advantage I see to the banks in allowing them to issue circulation as against gold, is this: At the present time, when they come up to the peak load, so to speak, of their circulation, they are afraid of ex- -ceeding the limit and of being fined, so they stop short of it. By depositing a certain amount of gold in this gold reserve, they will be relieved of that apprehension and the benefit will be that they can circulate to the extent of their paid pp capital, their emergency circulation and the amount of this deposit that they make. Consequently, there is less danger of the bank being fined and there will undoubtedly be an advantage to the public in getting increased circulation.

Did the committee consider the question of bank clerks' salaries? It Is a matter that has been discussed in the press and in which the public are interested to a large extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The committee did not
consider that question. Speaking for myself, I think it would be very difficult indeed to incorporate provisions in the Bank Act to deal with the question of salaries of bank employees. Banks carry on business in all parts of the world. The question of wages which they would pay would be determined by local and consequently by varying conditions. The question would arise as to the qualifications and abilities of the different employees. The matter is so complex that I doubt very much whether the House would be justified in attempting to introduce legislation dealing with it. So far as managers are concerned, my experience has been that they are underpaid, with the exception of managers of the head or principal offices. I do not wish to make a general statement as to that, but the men out in the firing line are not paid as well as they should be. The banks themselves should take the matter up and see that their employees are well paid, because it would be in their interest to do so. During the past few years there has been a considerable advance along that line, some of the banks being more generous than others. There seems to be some room for complaint that the ordinary bank clerks and managers in small branches are not paid as well as they should be. A provision was introduced by the committee that bank managers should not be allowed to engage in insurance or business of that kind. The idea is that they might use their position in order to force clients to insure with companies for which they might be agents for the purpose of mak

ing a commission for themselves. I have received some communications from bank managers protesting against that, on the ground that they are underpaid.

In regard to the question of the prohibition of managers from doing insurance business, I have had protests from bank managers in small towns and villages urging that it is an addition to their salaries, which are small. As the minister says, I do not believe that legislation could fix the salaries of these managers. Meanwhile could not the amendment, which we shall come to look into later on, be changed so as not to hurt bank officials in small villages and towns where the population is small and where the salary is correspondingly small?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we come to the other clause, that question will be dealt with.

I wish to say a word in support of what my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. McKay) has said, that there is a general belief that the salaries of bank employees, especially in the lower branches, are not as they should be. In evidence of that, it will be recalled that not very long ago-and I think the practice is still going on-certain of the banks systematically imported clerks from the Old Country. It may be said that the law of supply and demand should govern, and I am not going to say that you can advantageously interfere with that law in this particular instance. It has been found necessary in most mechanical employments for men to band themselves together in unions and to take measures in order to maintain a fair wage. Bank employees are not in a position to do that. While I do not know that those who are employed in banks are more entitled to sympathy than any others, that is one of the cases where it seems to me that a minimum wage should be established by law.
The public have an interest in this matter which they do not have in some other employments owing to the fact that bank employees, as a matter of fact handle the money of the country. It is necessary, for the proper protection of public business, that that money should be handled honestly. It is a recognized fact that there has been a considerable amount of dishonesty among the minor bank employees throughout Canada. It has been stated very frequently that that measure of dishonesty is largely due to the fact that these young men are underpaid considering the responsibilities of the duties which they have to perform and the conditions under which they are expected to live.

I am not so sure that
my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is giving the real reason for dishonesty on the part of certain bank clerks. Neither Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
am I so sure that bank clerks are not as well paid as clerks in other walks of life which require the same ability. If we could get it out of their heads that the burden is oast upon them to be social leaders in the towns and villages, perhaps we would get rid of some of the cry about the smallness of the salaries, and possibly in some cases take away the necessity of bank clerks becoming dishonest. I have no intention or desire to interfere with their social duties. I think bank clerks as a rule are pretty well paid.
Not the juniors.

I cannot agree with
that.
What is the hon. gentleman's experience as to salaries in banks?

I never was employed in a bank and I do not have a son in one. Not long ago a boy of about fifteen or sixteen years of age went into a bank. When I inquired what he was getting, I was told that, he was receiving $1.50 or $1.75 a day. I do not know in what other line of business he would earn anything like that in Canada at that age. Because a boy is in a bank which handles large sums of money, he seems to have an idea that he ought to get a large salary. The banks should not be judged harshly in this matter. I believe they are paying their clerks a pretty fair wage compared with what other business institutions are paying.

I do not think the junior
bank clerks are paid a sufficient salary. I understand that not only in the West but in the East as well, the junior clerks are paid only $250 a year.
It is $300 a year in the Bank of Montreal.

At any rate, I think the
general experience is that the salaries are not sufficient.

I do not think the
criticism that has been made with regard to the salaries of bank clerks is justifiable. The acceptance of a clerkship is a splendid opportunity for a young man sixteen or seventeen years of age to learn banking and business methods generally behind the counters of our foremost financial institutions. If there are dishonest bank clerks amongst the juniors, it is because there are too many facilities for their going to the bucket-shops in order to get rich quick. I think the Minister of Justice should attend to that end of the matter, and see that the brokers are not permitted to allow young men to dabble in stock-jobbing operations. In my experience as a practising lawyer and as Crown prosecutor in Montreal, I have found that the bucket-shops

and the brokers' offices are the places where the young bank clerks begin their fall. The young man of seventeen, eighteen or twenty years of age, who gets, as they get in the Bank of Montreal, $300 a year, with a yearly increase, cannot complain too much, after all. Having regard to the learned profession of the law, lawyers of undoubted ability, after a course of study of eight years at college and three or four at university, sometimes get less than $500 a year after they have been admitted to the Bar, and, after a practice of three or four years, the lawyer who gets $1,200 a year is very lucky. On the whole, therefore, I think that our young bank clerks cannot complain.

speechtext:

On section 88-loans upon live or dead stock; grain; cattle:

This clause
was not in the Bill as originally introduced, providing for the registration of security taken by the bank and considered in the abstract, I admit that it is very difficult to argue against that principle. My idea was that this amendment was perhaps more to meet transportation conditions in the West than a matter of banking. I have always been of the opinion that if this were confined to grain it would be only fair to all interests concerned for the bank to take its security and not to register it. I am still of the opinion that if it were

restricted to grain it would meet the demands of the West for the present and in that case it would not be necessary to have any registered security. As was pointed out in the Banking Committee on many occasions, the loans made by bankers are not ordinarily made on the security offered but rather on the character of the borrower. I cannot get rid of the apprehension that if borrowers are obliged to register their liens the section will be of little value to anybody. That is my own personal view. I know there is a very strong opinion to the contrary. If it were possible to restrict this to threshed grain, it would possibly meet the conditions in the West for some few years and eventually we could hope to see it stricken out of the Act altogether

I agree entirely with what has been said by the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). The purpose of the introduction of these two subsections, 2 and 3, was, as I mentioned previously, to give further bank facilities to the farmers in western Canada. We all know that in western Canada the time between the threshing of the grain and the closing of the season for doing fall work is very short. Ordinarily it does not exceed a month. If the farmer is obliged to haul out his grain for any long distance from his farm to the elevator or railway station, it occupies a great portion of his time and by reason of that he is not able to do his ploughing or other fall work which is necessary before the ground freezes up and he cannot do anything further on it. It is almost impossible for him to do his fall work if he has to haul that grain a distance of say five or six miles, but if it could be stored in his granary and if he could borrow on the security of his threshed grain so stored, the funds necessary for the payment of the employees who have helped him during the harvest and threshing time, it would give him an advantage which otherwise he would not have. It is quite consistent with the policy and principle of the Bank Act that advances or loans should be made on such security because it is of all the securities in the farmer's hands the most soluble, the most easily realizable. In addition to the advantage that it will give to the farmer in the way that I have mentioned there will also be the advantage that if he can store his grain on his farm during the winter months, and obtain a loan on it there he will save the elevator charges which otherwise he will have to pay if the grain remains in the country unshipped or unsold. As we all know a very large proportion of the grain does remain in the West because the farmers are unable to get it to the lake front for export before the season of navigation closes
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
It seems highly desirable that the farmers of the West should have the bank facilities provided by this Act, and power should be given to the banks to lend on this class of security, the best class of security and equal to the goods, wares and merchandise mentioned in other parts of the section upon which the bank makes advances.
Does the hon. gentleman think that it will be of any practical benefit to the farmer? If it will not be of any advantage to the farmer, it is better not to have it at all.

The evidence that was
given before the committee by men from the West showed that it was very important to the western farmer to have the privilege of borrowing from the bank on his threshed grain. It will be appreciated by him and the advantage that he will derive therefrom will be great. Now comes the other point of the registration of the lien. As I have pointed out, the loan can only happen after the grain is threshed. There can be no lien filed before that. The debts, the wages of those who have done the threshing, are all incurred prior to the threshing. Therefore, they are not incurred on the credit of the threshed grain. In order to pay these wages and obligations facilities should be given to the farmer to raise funds so that he will not be obliged to part with his grain at an inconvenient time, at a time when it will not be profitable for him and when he cannot obtain a suitable price. Consequently if the registration took place at the same time it would not be a protection to other creditors. It would not protect any of his creditors because his creditors have already given the credit and the debts have prior to the threshing of the grain been incurred. He then could raise the amount that the bank would feel disposed to advance to him to pay his creditors and in addition the creditors would have an equity of redemption in the pladged grain on which, if necessary, they could realize. If registration were made obligatory it would be inconsistent with the other parts of the Act because there is no lien required to be registered in any other section, and it would be discriminating against the farmer. The grain would be sold in the course of five or six months at the very utmost and therefore, to oblige the farmer to give a warning to others that he had raised money on his grain by registering the lien, would be unreasonable and unnecessary under the circumstances. It would also be expensive and is not required for Quebec. I hope that section concerning the registration will be struck out.

May I ask if this section would override the provincial legislation we have in the West whereby the thresher

would have a lien on the grain for a certain number of days.
I do not think so

It seems to
me it might.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The legal members of the committee were of opinion that the word ' remuneration ' in sub-section 8 of section 88 was sufficient to cover the point raised by my hon. friend. The matter brought to our attention by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is one about which there would be great difficulty in coming to a conclusion; you have to weigh the advantages on one hand and the disadvantages on the other. It is, I think, a sound principle in the legislation of the provinces that if the individual in visible possession of a property makes a mortgage of that property to secure a loan, publicity shall he given to the mortgage and hence we have in all the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, chattel mortgage legislation providing in substance that no security by way of chattel mortgage or bill of sale shall be valid as against creditors of the mortgagor unless registered in accordance with the legislation on that point. In Quebec a chattel mortgage of personal property is not valid and consequently there is no provision made for registration. The exception to that class of legislation which is general except in Quebec is contained in section 88 of the present Act, and in the interests of trade and commerce it has been found to be very beneficial. I think few if any abuses have grown up under it. The exception was made in the case of the wholelsale manufacturer or dealer and he was permitted to give a secret lien to the bank upon raw material, or product in progress of manufacture, or upon the manufactured article. That legislation is many years old. The lien that is given is not registered in accordance with the principle that exists in the chattel mort gage legislation of the several provinces. We now come to this particular section and I might say it was with very great reluctance that I introduced this provision giving a lien to the banker upon security of threshed grain because the whole principle underlying the Bank Act has been that the bank shall make its loans upon personal security: the standing and credit of the individual to whom the loan is made. Up to date, that has applied to every one with the single exception of the wholesale manufacturer or dealer to whom I have referred. By virtue of the provisions of section 88,_ he was entitled to borrow upon a secret lien. As I explained before, the reason, why we gave this privilege to the banks of lending money by way of bankers' liens upon threshed grain, was on account of the peculiar conditions existing in the 320
West which have been fully explained by my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Aikins), and of which all hon. members are well aware, namely, transportation, storage and the desirability that the farmer should not be obliged at once to throw his grain upon the market. That is the sole reason that led me to introduce this clause which widens the class from whom the secret lien may be taken. In the Bill as originally drafted, no provision was made for registration. I weighed, on the one hand, the disadvantage that might arise to creditors of the farmer, because it is possible that a creditor or creditors may be prejudiced by reason of the bank obtaining a lien unregistered upon threshed grain. On the other hand I had to weigh the advantage to the farmer who might desire to borrow in order to cope with conditions existing in the West. When the matter came up in committee, the question was discussed very fully, and I enunciated the view that my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has taken, stating that it would in my judgment, largely defeat the purpose we had in view if we compelled the registration of these liens, because I had been informed by the banks that in all probability, the clause would not be taken advantage of if the liens had to be registered. In the first place, I doubt if the banks would desire to lend as freely as they otherwise would. In the second place, the farmer would be put to some extra expense. In the third place, an exception has been made in the case of the province of Quebec, as hon. members will observe by looking at sub-section 9. I left the matter open to the committee, stating that I realized it was a question on which there might be a difference of opinion. It vvas not a political or controversial question in any narrow sense, and I simply expressed my view. The committee were of the opinion, I believe by a comparatively small majority, that it would be advisable that these liens should be registered. All I desire to say is that in the. House the matter is in the same position as it was in the committee. My view is that it is in the interest of die western farmer, whom this clause is designed to assist, that we should not insist upon the registration of the lien

When was
clause 36 put in? What were the reasons tor empowering banks to lend money to ranchers t Were the grounds given for that as strong as those in regard to lending money on threshed grain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, they were not The
reason given was this: The banks under existing legislation have been lending upon hankers' liens to cattle ranchers, that is to say, to men engaged in cattle raising in a wholesale way. They thought they were justified in doing that, particularly because of the wholesale idea involved. In other words, while they would not lend to a



farmer upon his cattle, they would lend to a rancher or a man engaged in the raising of cattle by wholesale. That is the existing practice to-day. Some doubt was thrown upon that practice by a decision in the Supreme Court of Alberta, I think, of Chief Justice Sifton. It was to make certain the banks' right to lend upon cattle to a rancher that this clause was first introduced. As I brought it down I think it did not go quite as far as this definition would imply; perhaps some words have been added in committee. It is unquestionably in the interest of the cattle-raising industry that the banks should have the right to take a lien, as they do in practice to-day. That principle applies now in section 88 with respect to threshed grain. I believe it is a sound banking principle that has underlain the Bank Act for forty years, that makes a bank Iook rather to the personal security of the farmer or the retailer; but where the wholesale principle exists, then it has been found by experience that the legislation had been beneficial, has served the needs and purposes of trade and commerce, especially in connection with the manufacturer and wholesaler. So far as I know, there have been no abuses by reason of lack ot publicity through want of registration. It would be unfortunate if the banks of Canada., because this legislation is general, should become chattel mortgagees of the personal property of small holders as well as large, and should have to resort to proceedings in the wav of selling out bv chattel mortgage sale in order to realize their security. In addition to that, the sound principle of banking is to loan upon a short date pro" missory note giving quick returns whioh prevents the locking up of money for a longer period. The tendency is to look to the chattel and its value rather than to the individual. That would lead probably to somewhat unsound banking and to a good deal of dissatisfaction in the_ community. It is entirely a matter of judgment, however, one way or the other, as to whether or not it is -advisable to register this lien.

Could we not have a
definition of the word 'rancher ? I think that point was raised, hut I thought there was some definition. On looking at the Bill, I find that the word ' farmer _ is defined, but the word ' rancher ' is not defined.

The word
[DOT] rancher' would not be susceptible of any exact definition in a Bill of this character. The history of the section is, shortly, this: The liens that hanks had under the common law not only extended to title deeds anrt securities that -were deposited with them, but were extended by decisions of the House of Lords to funds that a man might have in Mr WHITE (Leeds).
the bank. The banks had a habit of taking title deeds and securities from a person to whom they made a loan. When our statute was passed, we attempted to give a statutory lien that embodied the principle of the common Jaw lien that had grown up, instead of providing it by a chattel mortgage or a mortgage in form of a lien. We established in the original statute a lien known as Form C. That security carried with it all the rights that were given to a bank by reason of its common law lien that has grown up by the development of the common law through many years of history. I think originally it came from the Lombards and extended from there to the Old Country and came to us from London, England. Then, having given a statutory lien that was equivalent to the common law lien to which I have referred, the question was whether or not that should he extended to any parties other than wholesale dealers. If you look at the first portion of the section, you will find that it is expressly limited to:
Any wholesale purchaser or shipper of or dealer in products of agriculture, the forest, quarry and mine, or the sea, lakes and rivers, or to any wholesale purchaser or shipper of or dealer in live stock or dead stock or the products thereof, upon the security of such products, or of such live stock or dead or the products thereof.
In the case to which the Minister of Finance has referred the right of the bank to take a lien on a single horse was in issue. The trial judge held that this section did not apply, and that the security taken under section 88, from the farmer by the bank in relation to a single horse was illegal. Representations have from time to time been made by farmers and ranchers of the West as to the necessity for passing some legislation that would enable them to give security that would be practically of the same effect as the security given by their wholesale neighbours. I can only say that in the province of Alberta, where the larger ranching operations have been carried out, ranchers who have not sold a single animal by retail have been held to come within the terms of the first part of the section, and have been deemed to be wholesale dealers in live stock. That is to say, if a man had a large ranch with a thousand head of cattle on it he was warranted in giving the bank security under section 88 of the Bank Act, by reason of his being a wholesale dealer. If, on the other hand, he was a farmer who had about his premises perhaps one hundred head of cattle, the bank would decline to take that security because he was not a wholesale dealer, and the question arose as to how we could extend to that man the right to give security by what the Minister of Finance has described the creation of a secret lien, but which I prefer to designate merely

as the ordinary banker's lien extended by the operation of a statute. In my judgment sub-section 3 of section 88 should be amended, and I was going to suggest that it should be done because of the observation made by my hon. friend the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). We should say that the bank may lend money to a rancher or a farmer upon the security of his cattle, because the very difficulty that has been^ referred to in defining the word ' rancher ' will, as was suggested by the hon. member for Guysborough, be coming up every day in actual practice. I do not know of any definition of the word 'rancher' that could be considered applicable to the purposes of the statute. I understand that the hon. member for Red Deer is a rancher.
No.

Well, he is a farmer
now; when he came to this country he was a rancher. It is a fact that he has neighbours who are ranchers, and who do not call themselves farmers, although they may not have as many cattle as the horn gentleman has. On the one hand there may be a man who has twenty-five or thirty head of cattle and who calls himself a rancher, while on the other hand a man who claims to be a farmer may have one hundred head of cattle. If we concede that the bank is to lend money under section 88 of the Bank Act to other than wholesale dealers, in my judgment that privilege should be extended not only to the farmer upon his grain, but to the mixed farmer upon his cattle, as well as to the rancher. It was because of the difficulty suggested by my hon. friend the member for Guysborough that I was going to ask the committee to insert in this clause the words ' or farmer,' to make the clause read:
The bank may lend money to a rancher or farmer upon the security of his cattle.
The question of my hon. friend was, what is a rancher?

I would say that in
practice a rancher is one who raises live stock and cultivates his farm lands, if there be any, in order to supply grain and fodder for his cattle, and not for the purpose of selling the grain as a product of his farm. Is that not a fair definition?

It is a long
one.

You cannot define it
shorter. You cannot say a rancher is one who deals in cattle; that would not be sufficient. He is more than a raiser of cattle; he raises stock upon his farm and cultivates an area for the purpose only of supplying food for his stock. A mixed farmer, on the other hand, is a man whose
320.}
primary business is farming, who cultivates his farm for the purpose of raising cereals or other crops for sale, and who incidentally raises cattle. If I recollect aright, in some of the cases that arose in the United States, the word * rancher ' was defined as applying to a man whose primary business was the raising of cattle.

Why not strike out
the word ' rancher ' altogether, and say that the company may lend money to persons engaged in the raising of live stock?

That was discussed in the committee; that is already conceded by the first part of the section; the bank has the right to lend money to the wholesale dealer in live stock. I am, perhaps, more familiar with the practical than the theoretical side of the question. I know that some of the banks in western Canada of which I have an intimate knowledge have been in the habit of taking from ranchers security under section 88 of the Bank Act in cases where the ranchers did not sell only one or two head of cattle at a time, but rather dealt in wholesale quantities. [DOT]
What was the point and the decision in the case referred to?

The issue turned upon the question of interest, which was applicable to another section, and as to whether or not in the exercise of its rights under the chattel mortgage, the bank could charge [DOT] more or less than is provided by statute for the services rendered in connection with selling the cattle under the chattel mortgage. I submit that if we are going to extend the right to deal with cattle under section 3 of the Bank Act, we should at least say that the farmer who has twenty or fifty head of . cattle should have just the same rights as the man whom we call a rancher, and who may have no more cattle than he has. If that be so the best method to express it is for the committee to consider. As I remember that question did arise in committee and there was considerable discussion of it and the suggestion of my hon. friend from Macdonald was considered that all these words should be struck out and we should simply leave it ' a bank may lend money upon the security of live stock.' That is true now but it applies only to the wholesaler. The reason that that is now safe is that we have in the West a brand law and under the criminal code a brand upon the side of an animal is prima facie evidence of ownership; and when the bank takes such cattle as security under section 88, with the registered brand of that owner, such animals are the property of the bank, and if anyone exercised acts of ownership over such animals other than the registered owner there would be a

prima facie case against him. So a bank lending money to a rancher on the security of his live stock is safe. Registration of the security, I think, would serve no useful purpose, and in fact, in my personal view, would destroy the practical value of the provision.

I wish that
my hon. friend had defined the word 'rancher.' I find it in the Century dictionary, which applies to the United States, that the word is so defined that in my opinion the word farmer would include it. I believe that the word farmer wouid apply to every kind of tilling of the soil or getting anything from the soil.

In New Mexico they
do not refer to farms at all, and in parts of British Columbia and in Montana they speak of different kinds of farms, fruit farms &c. as ranches. On the plains of Alberta in the early days they referred to them all as ranches, but that word has now been replaced by 'farms.' The word ' farm ' is not comprehensive enough to cover ' ranch.' I think that the word ranch is used in practice very much in Canada.
I wish to make a suggestion that in defining farmer we say that farmer includes rancher.
That would cover it.

And allow the farmer
to borrow on his grain and cattle.

Of course we do not
undertake to define farmer, we simply say that it includes certain things. I said I do not believe that registration would serve any useful purpose. Neither the farmer nor the banker desires to have registration of chattel mortgages or securities of this character.

What about the trader
who sells to the farmer, not knowing of the existence of such a lien?

That is no more than the ordinary banker's lien is to-day. The trader has no knowledge of it, it is a statutory development of a common law principle! A farmer has certificates of ownership of his property. He goes in to the bank, he has no grain or stock on his property and he says to the banker: I desire to discount a note for $1,000; I have nothing to give you as security under section 88 of the Bank Act, but I hand you my certificates of title to my real estate. That is thereby constituted a banker's lien.

I would rather think that is' an attempt to lend money on the security cf real estate.
Mr. BENNETT (Calsarv'

In this case there
would be no negotiation at the time, but the bank would take it subsequently or even at the time as collateral security.

He could not make a
loan of that kind from the bank.
The banks do not take that at the time of negotiating, but they take it right afterwards as collateral security for the advance that has been made.

I thought my hon.
friend meant that they were taken simultaneously.

That might be under
the Torrens title, but in our province we would not refer to the certificate of title but would go to the registry office.

The only thing is that
the man in the maritime provinces who would attempt to make a sale under those conditions would be liable under the criminal code.

Some one is
punished anyway.

Yes. In the case of a
loan on cattle borrower executes the pledge. Form C, when he makes the loan. There must be a contemporaneous pledging.

On
