speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think I have
quite made myself clear. This matter has been discussed, I think, on previous occasions in this House. I think it was discussed in 1891 and in 1901, and the conclusion was come to, I believe, that it was not desirable legislation that the ordinary farmer engaged in mixed farming should be allowed to give to the bank a lien upon the security of his live stock. The committee, I believe, affirmed that view, that, so far as the farmer in Nova Scotia or Ontario was concerned, it would not be good legislation that he should give to the banks what is in effect a chattel mortgage upon his live stock. The intention of this sub-section 3 of section 88 was, as I pointed out before, to meet the case of the wholesale cattle raiser. The words ' wholesale cattle raiser ' are not a very accurate definition of the class of people engaged in the raising of cattle to whom the banks have made loans in the past upon receiving a banker's lien, and, therefore, the word * rancher ' was intended to represent the description of the person engaged in cattle raising on a wholesale scale, to whom the bankers had in the past made
10:29

advances upon a lien upon their cattle. There are two matters to be considered, first is it advisable to give the bankers the privilege of taking, upon the security of their cattle, a lien from the farmers all over Canada. On more than one occasion this House has decided that that would not be good legislation, having regard to the principle I referred to a little while ago that the banks should look to the standing and reputation of the firm or person to whom it lends, and not to a chattel mortgage security. If the committee is of opinion that we should depart from that principle and give to the bank the privilege of taking a lien from mixed farmers upon the security of their live stock, then the question of registration becomes a very live and important question.
It seems to be conceded now that the banks should have a lien upon the farmer's property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as threshed grain
is concerned, they took that view, but so far as live stock is concerned, they took the view I am now giving. My right hon. friend has probably a different definition of ' rancher ' from what the committee had. The committee had the idea that a' rancher meant a person engaged in the wholesale raising of cattle, and not in mixed farming. There are two things to be considered, first whether it is desirable to give mixed farmers all over Canada the right to give to the bank a lien upon their live stock. If that is not advisable, I submit that we should not put in the word ' farmer ' in sub-section 3. It may be necessary to define the word * rancher ' so as to cover the class of people I have mentioned, and as it is a matter of very great importance I would suggest that we have a pronouncement upon the question of registration of the security, and by the time this comes up again I will see if it is possible to give any definition of * rancher,' or otherwise to describe the class of person we have in mind.
If I understand my hon. friend correctly, he said he agreed to the farmer giving security upon his threshed grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

But he will
not allow the same man to give security upon his cattle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is my view.
May I ask the reason why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The reason is this:	we
have given the farmer the right to give security upon his threshed grain under a banker's lien by reason of the exceptional
considerations which prevail in the West in respect to transportation and storage. These considerations, which make that desirable, do not arise in the case of cattle or live stock, and we have to have regard to the situation existing in other provinces, to the rights of creditors, and to the other matters that I have mentioned. As to the inadvisability of banks becoming really chattel mortgagees on live stock of the farmers all over the country, 1 am aware that the argument has been put forward very strongly upon the occasion of the two last revisions of the Act, and the sense of the Llouse in the past has been against it, for the reasons I have given.

I agree to a very large
extern with my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), in regard to the difficulties as to the definition of a rancher and farmer which surround this section. I think that in passing the Act in this way you are leaving yourselves open to create a good deal of trouble for the banks and the borrowers. It is a matter which will bring about a considerable amount of litigation. The whole question seems to centre round whether you will or will not have registration. The theory is advanced by the Minister of Finance that registration means . that the banks will not lend money as freely and that it will entail consideraoie expense to the farmer. With neither of these propositions am I prepared to agree. I cannot understand why the bank should refuse to lend money on something that is to them an absolute security. That security will De enhanced by reason of the registration, and as for the expense, it would be merely nominal. What I wished to refer to particularly, however, was that you are using the argument that the banks should have a secret lien while by this section you are not giving it to them, because no time is provided for registration. If the right is to be given to the bank to lend upon this class of security, surely, as in the chattel mortgage Acts, there ought to be a time given for registration of the security upon which the money is advanced.

It is only
valid when registered.

It might be held back
as a secret sale.

If you are going to put
through a section of this kind, you certainly ought to have a time limit within which the security ought to be registered or filed. It seems to me to be the gist of the whole section. You are endeavouring to do something, and you are not doing it at all.

I have not
yet been convinced, and I doubt if the Committee on Banking and Commerce were convinced, that this is very good legislation to start with. I doubt the advisability of giving bankers the power to lend

money to farmers or ranchers on the security of horses or cattle, but if we are going to do so, I do not see why the lien should not be registered for the reason advanced by my hon. friend for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) that the tradesmen and any other men who 'have 'been giving credit to the farmer in the past ought to be protected just as well as the banks. They tell us that the banks lend money to their customers on personal credit, that a man can go into a bank and get what money he requires if his face is a letter of credit. He does not need to give any secret lien. Therefore this legislation must be advanced for the purpose of assisting the man who has not that personal credit, who is either dishonest, or so hard up that he is liable to become dishonest. It opens up an entirely new avenue for fraud. I am opposed to these two sections for that reason. I know it was asked for by the western farmers, but the committee had at least one memorial, in which the Grain Growers' Association, in the neighbourhood of Saltcoats, Saskatchewan, I think, asked that it should not go into effect. I think that we would perhaps save ourselves a good deal of the trouble of wrangling over these smaller points if we were to decide at first whether it was possible to put this legislation into effect at all.

I agree with my hon.
friend from North Bruce (Mr. Clark), although I cannot see any reason why a bank should not be allowed to lend money to a farmer on his threshed grain or on his stock if it wants to do so. The bank, as a rule, does not lend money to the ordinary individual. It requires something else. I know that in large transactions, men who are dealing in large amounts of money, are probably able to go to the bank and get a certain amount of credit themselves, but this legislation is not intended to help that class of borrower. It is the small man, the man who wants $200 or $300 to whom this legislation will apply. In the portion of Canada that I know anything about a man, in order to procure a loan, has to get an endorser. No man can go to the bank and get money unless he is prepared to go around bothering his neighbours or friends in order to find an endorser.

It is very
rarely that the banks ask for an endorser.

The hon. gentleman
should go down East. In New Brunswick you could not get $25 on your note without an endorser. Talk about getting money without an endorser!
I am referring to farmers.

They want your wife's
name on the note also, especially if they suspect that she has a little money in the savings bank. It may be all right in Ontario but it will not be down East. I see Mr. CLARK (North Bruce).
no reason why banks should not be allowed to advance money to a farmer on his cattle or his grain. If they are allowed to do that then I submit that they have no right to do it by a secret lien or mortgage. They make that loan the same as I would or the same as any man who loans money. If I want to take a lien upon a man's horse I must record it within a certain number of days or hours. It would be all right between the borrower and myself but as between the borrower and an innocent third party, or a judgment creditor, the lien is of no value unless it is recorded. I do not see Why a bank should be placed in any different position from that of any other lender. If a bank lends money and takes that security it should be required to record that evidence of title the same as any other lender would be. However, I do not think this will' cut any figure one way or the other. I doubt very much if the banks will loan money to a farmer on his threshed grain or his live stock. I cannot see any objection to compelling them to record their evidence of title. I would not find any fault if the whole thing were eliminated. I do not think it would do the farmers of the West any good, but I believe that it is only holding out to the people of the West a false hope that it will be a benefit to them when it will not be because the banks will come back to the personal security and if they are afraid of the personal security they will ask for an endorser. I do not care whether you elminate the whole thing or not.

Would you place the
farmer in a different position from that occupied by the wholesale merchant? I understand that it is not necessary to register the security of the wholesale merchant.

I do not think that a
wholesale merchant will come under the provision of section 88. It is applicable rather to the manufacturer of lumber and people of that class. Then, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), if it is extended to the Wholesale dealer in live stock you encounter a difficulty in interpreting the words ' farmer ' and ' rancher.' That is the difficulty which seems to have led to this discussion. I quite agree with the hon. member for Calgary as to the difficulty of intelligently interpreting the words * farmer ' or ' rancher.' I do not believe it is possible. The hon. gentleman gave a splendid illustration. He took a man living in Red ' Deer, my friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), who would be classified as a farmer. Another gentleman living alongside of him does not have as much stock as he has yet he would be classified as a rancher. There you see the difficulty. I strongly contend that it will be a great mistake if you leave section 88 as it is; it will lead to great difficulty if you do not strike out the word

' rancher.' I believe you ought give this privilege to the farmer as well as to the rancher and I would not feel very much aggrieved if you took it away from both.

I wish to put on record my proposal so that if the minister redrafts the section he will have the benefit of it. Assuming that this committee is in favour of retaining sub-clauses 2 and 3 of section 88, my proposal is that we amend sub-section (G) of the Interpretation Act by adding the words ' or ranch ' so as to make it read:
Farmer, includes the owner, occupier, landlord and tenant of a farm or ranch.
That dispenses with the use of the word ' rancher ' later on. Then I would amend section 88 by striking out sub-clauses 2 and 3 and substituting:
2.	The bank may ilend money to a farmer:
(a) Upon the security of his threshed grain grown upon his farm;
(h) Upon the security of his cattle.
That would make it clear, and we would have no difficulty as between the words * farmer ' and ' rancher.' I agree that if we are to make this concession it ought to be registered. My difficulty is that the registry offcers in the different provinces are provincial officers and it would be quite open to a registry officer if his friend were interested agaist the bank to refuse to accept the document. He would be liable to no penalty if he did refuse. The provinces prescribe regulations as to the indexing and filing of different documents that are required to be registered under provincial law, but these regulations would not necessarily apply to the documents filed by the bank. I suppose we could not provide that such officers .should keep a registry book so that a person going to the bank to search would be able to find out whether a certain farmer did mortgage his grain or his cattle to the hank. I would like to be informed as to how these difficulties may be overcome.

If a
chattel mortgage were given under the Bank Act in Nova Scotia, could the provincial registrar refuse to record the mortgage?
We are passing federal legislation and we have no power to compel that officer to receive or register this document at all.

In Ontario, and it
would doubtless be the same in Nova Scotia, a provincial law could not override a Dominion law on banking, and the bank is not obliged to register what otherwise would be a chattel mortgage, because the Dominion Act does not require it to do so. Any other lender but a bank, in doing the same thing and taking a chattel mortgage,
would have to register it within five days. That is where the anomaly comes in.

The committee should strike out the clause altogether or else leave it in and insist upon a proper filing and regisration. It is a very dangerous principle to allow a bank or anybody else to take secret liens or securities to the detriment of others. In the United States there is no such system as .a secret lien under their banking laws.

Would not my hon. friend be satisfied if we struck out sub-clause 3 and left clause 2 without registration? That would give to the farmer of the West the advantage it was intended to give him of raising money on his threshed grain.

I would not wish my
opinion to prevail with regard to any condition existing in the West. I am speaking of the conditions in Ontario and as they would affect my own constituents. If clauses 2 and 3 are to remain, I cannot see why the bank should not be allowed to loan, not only upon security of threshed grain upon the farm and to the rancher upon the security of his cattle, but also to the farmer upon the security of his live stock. My amendment which I moved in committee and which was voted down, would include the Ontario farmer, whose money is invested largely in cattle, horses, and hogs; it would give him an opportunity to get a loan from the bank to carry him over the period of marketing his stock. Mr. Powell, who was manager of a bank in Weyburn, deposed that he would lend to no person with a lien to whom he would not loan without a lien; he would lend on the personal character of the borrower. He, with others, was totally opposed to secret liens; he testified that in the interests of the general public the lien should be filed and registered for public notification. In the province of Ontario landlords will be prejudiced by the operation of this lien, because this law would over-ride provincial legislation, which gives the landlord a priority under the Landlords and Tenants Act.
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax); Are you sure of that?

I argued in the committee that in legislation where the Dominion has undoubted jurisdiction its law would over-ride the law of the province, and it will give the bank priority over the landlord, and Mr. Wallace Nesbitt, counsel for the bankers, agrees with my contention.

Would not the effect
be that the lien which we allow the farmer

to give to the bank would be worked out under the laws of the province?
No.

We have no power to
interfere with property and civil rights.
Yes, we have, where we have jurisdiction.

Where security is given
in pursuance of Dominion legislation in matters over which we have exclusive jurisdiction, in my opinion there is no doubt that would take priority over a landlord's lien. I would suggest, if we are going to allow this in the Bill, that the lien to the bank should be subject to all the priorities now given under the legislation of the provinces. This committee should stand by the matured deliberation and judgment of the Banking and Commerce Committee, which, after careful consideration of the evidence submitted came to the conclusion that this clause should remain in order to extend the facilities for loaning, but at the same time I believe the lien should be registered so that the public should not be prejudiced by the existence of such lien.

The western farmer
has been getting considerable advice in this House and out of it to the effect that he should go in for mixed farming. Since this Bill has been introduced in the House, I have had occasion to talk with bankers in western Canada. They think the provision for the farmer should include not only threshed grain but live stock. In the interpretation clause of cattle, hogs are left out. In my part of the country, farmers who go in for mixed farming, go in almost wholly for hog-raising, and raise very few cattle or sheep. I think hogs should be included in order to enable the farmer who goes in for mixed farming to raise money on his hogs. In my part of the country, a rancher is known as a person distinct from a farmer. A rancher is a man engaged absolutely in raising live stock; any hay or grain that he raises is simply for his stock. I have the opinion of bankers that such a provision would be along the right line and would assist farmers by enabling them to borrow money on their live stock.

I would suggest that sub-section 3 of section 88 be amended by striking out the words in line 35, 'to a rancher,' and in the last line, ' his cattle,' and substituting therefor the word ' livestock.' That would make the clause read in this way:
The bank may lend money upon the security of live stock.
Mr. CARVELL.
As regards the matter of registration, I was not a member of the Banking Committee. but I am absolutely in favour of the idea that a lien of this kind should be registered. I would consider it eminently unfair to creditors of a farmer or any man, who might secure a loan from a bank under this Act, that he should do so privately without registration and to the detriment of creditors who had previous claims against him. The clause should stay in with that registration clause added, and some clause should be inserted whereby the registration would be according to the laws of the province in which the registration occurred, with the same safeguard. When I use the word safeguard, it means that, if a man gives a chattel mortgage upon his cattle with intent to defraud his creditors, that mortgage is null and void with regard to the province of Ontario and may be annulled. I think the banks should be in the same position with regard to a chattel mortgage in this or any other province where a loan has been negotiated.

At first glance, I did
not quite agree with my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) on the question of landlords' rights, but on a moment's reflection I think he is probably correct. If this clause remains as it is, the rights of a landlord will be very seriously jeopardized in the case of a dishonest tenant. In my county, and I suppose in every county in Ontario, there are hundreds of retired farmers who have come to the cities and towns, and who are dependent upon the rentals of their farms which they have retained. If it is possible for a tenant to pledge his grain and stock to a bank and thus deprive, the landlord of the right to distrain in order to collect his rent, it is a most serious matter. A dishonest tenant could realize by loan on his stock or grain, leave the farm and thus leave the landlord in the lurch. He cannot do it now, because the landlord can seize as soon as he sees any evidence that the tenant desires to leave the farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend see
any objection to loaning to farmers throughout Canada on a lien, whether registered or unregistered?
I do not think registration would help in this case, because if the bank registered a lien, it would come against the landlord. I would rather see the clause struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has come upon one of the many reasons which have influenced the House in the past to decline to allow the lien to be given in respect of live stock owned by farmers. I desire to point out further for the consideration of the committee that in the province of

Quebec there is no machinery for registration at all. The banks aTe all in favour of getting permission to loan money on live stock owned by farmers, as my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) has said. They desire to get all the security they can. If in the province of Quebec the right is given to a farmer to borrow upon his live stock, there can be no provision for registration there, because there a chattel mortgage is not required to be registered and there is no machinery for registration. The result will be that the banks will have liens upon live stock of the farmers of Quebec, possibly to the prejudice of their landlords and other creditors. It is a very difficult question. The view reached was that it would not be good legislation to extend this privilege to farmers all over Canada, although a good many arguments in favour of it might be advanced. The discussion has been a very useful one. Personally I would like the clause to stand over in order to see if it is possible to give such a definition of the wholesale cattle raiser in the West as would get over the difficulty raised by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). He and others have clearly shown that in the West it is difficult to say who is a farmer and who is a rancher. It is very difficult to give a definition that will make clean-cut the distinction. If the committee will allow the clause to stand over, I shall be glad to give it further consideration and endeavour to reach some satisfactory definition.

I was going
to ask my hon. friend what was the meaning of the provision at the end of subsection 9, which says:
Provided that this sub-section shall not apply in the province of Quebec.
You can eliminate that provision, not because in the province of Quebec chattel mortgages are not required to be registered, but because chattel mortgages do not exist in that province. The pledge in the province of Quebec to be valid must be accompanied by delivery to the mortgagee. Therefore there is no necessity for this provision. If you say, as it says here, that sub-section 9 shall not apply in the province of Quebec, the consequence will be that the farmer in Quebec will be able to give a secret lien without registration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the farmer is given the privilege, which he is not, as the Bill is drafted.

You provide
in sub-section 8 that the farmer can pledge his grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: His threshed grain, not his cattle.

This pledge to be valid everywhere must be registered except in the province of Quebec. The consequence is that in the province of Quebec the farmer can pledge his grain without registration, and the creditors of the farmer are exposed to loss because they will find a secret lien upon the property of their debtor. That is another difficulty which has not been looked into, and which is very serious indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
will recall that when the Bill was first presented to the House there was no provision for registration in any of the provinces. When the committee decided that the lien should be registered then, as there was no machinery in the province of Quebec for effectuating registration, that proviso was inserted, otherwise the liens could not have been taken by the banks in the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has brought up another difficulty which I discussed before the Banking and Commerce Committee: that is as to whether the Dominion has jurisdiction to compel an official of the provincial government to register, because the offices for the registration of chattel mortgages in the several provinces are provincial. My own view is that the Dominion has such jurisdiction; I think the Dominion can order a certain person to do a certain act, persona designata; therefore I do not think that objection is a valid one. In the case of any one bank it was declared that the Dominion had jurisdiction by reason of the Bank Act coming within the provisions of section 91 of the British North America Act. With regard to the other point raised by my hon. friend with regard to registration in the province of Quebec, it is perfectly clear that as chattel mortgages do not exist in that province, and no machinery for registration has been provided, it will not be possible to carry out the recommendations of the committee as to registration in that province. If the privilege of borrowing upon the security of their live stock is given to mixed farmers all over Ganada, I think that the securities should be registered, but right at the outset are all these difficulties with regard to the granting of this privilege. The first question to be settled- is, it seems to me, having regard to all the questions which have been raised and the considerations which have been mentioned-whether the farmer is. engaged in extensive or in comparatively small and unimportant operations ; whether he has a thousand cattle or but one-whether it is good legislation to give the farmer the right to pledge to the bank his live stock as security for a loan. In coming to a conclusion, regard should be had to the argument advanced by the hon.

member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie)-which I think was a very strong one -that landlords would be prejudiced and would probably take chattel mortgages to protect themselves; that creditors would be prejudiced, and that in the province of Quebec the chattel mortgage is unknown. These are the considerations which seem to me to bear on the question as to whether we shall extend to the farmer the privilege of borrowing upon his live stock.

I said that
I thought it was not desirable to compel registration of the security taken by the banks under this section, if it merely provided for the loaning of money upop grain to meet western conditions, and I still adhere to that. I do not think registration would be necessary, or that it would serve any useful purpose. There is clearly a distinction between advances made upon grain and advances made upon cattle. I rise chiefly to make the suggestion to the minister that he take into consideration between now and Monday whether the old clause should not remain in the Bank Act instead of the amendments which were inserted by him when the Bill was presented. Personally I cannot see that they will serve any useful purpose to the citizens of this country; on the contrary they are surrounded by very many difficulties, and I think the minister should give the matter his careful attention and, I hope, come to the conclusion that it would be better to withdraw these amendments altogether.

This clause, as I understand it, was introduced largely for the benefit of tbe western gram grower. As was stated by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) there is a period of stringency -a period of from thirty to sixty days-between the time the crop is gathered in and the time it can be sold and placed upon the market. I think there was a unanimous desire on the part of the committee to help the western farmer to such an extent that he would not be forced to drop his work before his crop was entirely harvested for the purpose of selling a certain amount of grain to meet immediate liabilities. It was thought, therefore, that if the farmer had the right to borrow money for a certain period of time, say thirty or sixty days, it would make matters easier for him until such time as he could place his grain upon the market to better advantage. Of course this led to further difficulties, which have already been dwelt upon. I quite agree with a good deal of what has been said by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) to the effect that we are perhaps giving rise to as many difficulties with regard to the farmers of the other provinces as we are extending benefits to the farmers of the West. I desire to draw Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
the attention of the committee to the latter part of subsection 2:
The bank may lend money to a farmer upon the security of his threshed grain grown upon the farm.
What is the idea of inserting the words ' grown upon the farm.' If a farmer in Ontario wants to raise money, it is very likely that he will raise it upon grain that has not been grown upon his farm. Suppose for instance, there is a large amount of damaged wheat in the West, and one of the farmers in Ontario, who has a large amount of stock during the season, desires in October or November to buy a carload of damaged grain to feed his stock through the winter. Under this clause, as I understand it, he would be prohibited from getting a loan from the bank on the grain which he considered he had been obliged to buy to carry his stock through the winter. If he is the possessor of grain and has got it in his granary, surely that is all the banker requires. Why should the farmer be obliged to prove that his grain has been grown upon his farm? That applies not only to wheat, but to western corn. Many of our farmeis in Ontario buy a large amount of western corn to feed their hogs and cattle. If there is a time when they are likely to require an advance, it is when they are laying in enough feed to carry their stock through the winter season. I do not think that any useful purpose can be served by these words ' grown upon the farm.' I have not heard the minister refer to them, but it is clear that these words can in no way enhance the bankers security, and are a distinct disadvantage to the farmer if he has been obliged to purchase grain from his neignbour for the purpose of feeding his stock.
There would not be much security afforded by that grain if it were eaten by the cattle the next day.

The farmer has to
prove that the grain is there or he cannot get the advance. The average farmer in Ontario feeds his grain, whether it is grown upon the farm or whether it is bought. Whether the grain he possesses has been grown upon his own farm or whether it has been purchased from his neighbour or from the grain grower in the West, why should he be debarred from pledging, as security for a loan, grain that has been bought as well as grain that has been grown upon his own farm? I think myself that the difficulty that has been caused through the introduction of these sections counterbalances any good that we will be able to do to the western grain growers. I doubt whether it will be largely taken advantage of and if it is it will lead to complications in other provinces. I do not think the Act would suffer very much jf those two clauses were omitted; but if they remain I do not think

it necessary that the grain should be only grain raised on his own farm.

The clause that appears in the Act at present is especially drafted for western conditions but it is well to remember that with-the exception of the province of Quebec its application i3 general. Our experience in western Ontario is that where a man is engaged in the live stock business he has little or no difficulty in securing a loan from the bank to carry on his business. It is not an uncommon thing for a farmer to grass forty or fifty head of cattle and to ship a carload. In that case he would come under the description of a wholesaler, and in my opinion the amendments as drafted are unnecessary and will lead to considerable trouble.

In the afternoon I drew
attention to the definition of cattle in section 2 and asked that whatever might be the intention of the Government there should be a definition of the word ' rancher.' Since we have come to the discussion of section 88 I want to say that as we have now come to the principle of the question I would go a great deal further than I did in the afternoon when we were only discussing the definition. In the afternoon I explained why it was desirable from my point of view that there should be a definition of the intention of the Act, and of its scope. As it stands at present it carries on its face an injustice and a discrimination against the farmers of the part of the West which I represent and which I think, for the credit of the minister and of his legislation, it is desirable should be removed. But on the merits of the question I agree with the hon. member for Brandon wiien he explained the peculiar and special conditions existing in the Western country which makes it very desirable in the interest of the farmer himself in regard to the matter of transportation and in every other way that he should be enabled to realize or partially realize on his grain at the earliest possible date. That being conceded, the condition is entirely different in regard to live stock. The special conditions that prevail with regard to grain do not prevail with regard to livestock; and when the minister sees fit to introduce the provision regarding live stock it must be for reasons other than and different from those which exist in regard to grain. I shall not discuss the propriety or necessity of introducing this provision in regard to live stock, that is .here on the responsibility of the minister and of the Government, and it is to their credit if it is beneficial and it is to the contrary if it is not beneficial.

Is the
hon. member in favour of the principle of the legislation?
I do not wish to express any opinion as to the principle.
I think we are entitled to his opinion.

I have given my opinion in regard to the grain. In my opinion the principle of the legislation with regard to grain is desirable; the conditions in regard to live stock are entirely different. The same conditions do not exist and I do not express any opinion in regard to live stock, I do not express an opinion in regard to the principle underlying the legislation with respect to live stock. If it is considered by the Government desirable to make provision such as contained in this section in regard to live stock, that provision should be applicable to all live stock and there should not be a distinction between the rancher and the farmer. My views were expressed very clearly by the hon. member for Parry Sound in the amendment which he proposed, as it struck me that that would be a satisfactory expression of the idea if it is intended to be adhered to. I wish to strongly emphasize my objection to the principle that has been expressed by the minister of drawing a distinction between the rancher and the farmer. He admits himself that such a distinction is difficult to draw in words. I must say that it is still more difficult to draw in actual facts. There is no reason, so far as I can see, from any point of view why there should be a distinction and there are many reasons why there should not. If there is any advantage in the permission to the banks to advance money in regard to live stock, from every point of view the mixed farmer of the Northwest is entitled to that advantage. He is the man who can give the banks the best security and the sort of farming that he is carrying on is entitled to the greatest encouragement at the hands of this Parliament. There is no interest that can possibly suffer, so far as I can see, by giving to him that advantage if it is to be given to anybody in regard to live stock.
As to registration, I would say that in regard to advances on grain it is quite possible that the conditions are such as have been suggested by the hon. member for Brandon, that the security taken on grain would not, in the public interest, require to be registered. On the other hand, I would say that undoubtedly if there is to be a security taken on live stock that security should be registered. I think it would be a fair suggestion to make. the lien without registration of grain, and with registration of live stock, as suggested by the hon. member for Parry Sound.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If granted at all.

I am not offering any suggestion on that point. I understand there are good reasons why it should be granted. There may be reasons against it being granted, but I am not familiar with them. The same reasons do not exist in regard to cattle, as in regard to grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will consider it at
the next session of the committee. I am afraid we shall not be able to make further progress to-night on account of the absence of many hon. members who took a keen interest in these matters in the Committee on Banking and Commerce. I therefore move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
The following sections stand: 2, 43, 54, 55, 56, 56a, 76, 77, 88, 91, 93, 94, 99, 112, 117, 146.
Progress reported.

Monday, May 19, 1913.
